solution_info.solution_info:
Let $r$ be the radius of $C_{4}$. Let the point $P_{k}$ be the center of $C_{k}$ for $1 \leq k \leq 4$. Let $A$ be the point of intersection of circles $C_{1}$ and $C_{4}$ and let $\ell$ be the tangent line to $P_{1}$ at $A$. By symmetry, $P_{3}$ is the midpoint of $\overline{P_{1} P_{2}}$, and $P_{1} P_{3}=\frac{1}{4}$. Also by symmetry, $P_{4}$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{P_{1} P_{2}}$. The radius $\overline{P_{1} A}$ is perpendicular to $\ell$. Likewise the radius $\overline{P_{4} A}$ is perpendicular to $\ell$, so $P_{1}, P_{4}$, and $A$ all lie on the segment $\overline{P_{1} A}$ with $P_{4}$ between $P_{1}$ and $A$. Then $P_{1} P_{4}=1-r$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/d27ebeda9e584f5fa5833bb5f9af87bca5b0fa40e4f0a98ab15dfee76a66e0c0.jpg]

The radius of $C_{3}$ is $\frac{3}{4}$. Then $P_{3} P_{4}=\frac{3}{4}+r$, and $\triangle P_{1} P_{3} P_{4}$ is a right triangle with $P_{1} P_{3}=\frac{1}{4}$, $P_{3} P_{4}=\frac{3}{4}+r$, and $P_{1} P_{4}=1-r$. By the Pythagorean Theorem,

$\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{3}{4}+r\right)^{2}=(1-r)^{2}$
Expanding gives

$\frac{1}{16}+\frac{9}{16}+\frac{3 r}{2}+r^{2}=1-2 r+r^{2}$
which gives $r=(\text{D})\boxed{\frac{3}{28}}$.

raw_content.title:
What is the product of all solutions to the equation

$\log _{7 x} 2023 \cdot \log _{289 x} 2023=\log _{2023 x} 2023?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Changing the logarithms to base $b=2023=7.289$ using the Change of Base Formula gives

$\frac{1}{\log _{b} 7 x} \cdot \frac{1}{\log _{b} 289 x}=\frac{1}{\log _{b} b x} .$
It follows that $\log _{b} 7 x \cdot \log _{b} 289 x=\log _{b} b x$. Let $y=\log _{b} x$. It is possible to rewrite this equation as

$\left(y+\log _{b} 7\right)\left(y+\log _{b} 289\right)=y+1 .$
Note that $\log _{b} 7+\log _{b} 289=1$. Expanding the quadratic equation and simplifying gives

$y^{2}+y+\left(\log _{b} 7 \cdot \log _{b} 289\right)=y+1 .$
Then $y^{2}=1-\log _{b} 7 \cdot \log _{b} 289>0$, so there are two solutions for $y$, which can be denoted as $y_{1}$ and $y_{2}=-y_{1}$. Setting $x_{i}=b^{y_{i}}$ (for $i=1,2$ ) gives $x_{1} x_{2}=b^{y_{1}+y_{2}}=b^{0}=1$. Hence the requested product is $(\text{C})\boxed{1}$.

Note: The solutions to the given equation are approximately 943.8 and its reciprocal.

raw_content.title:
Rows $1,2,3,4$, and $5$ of a triangular array of integers are shown below:

Each row after the first row is formed by placing a $1$ at each end of the row, and each interior entry is $1$ greater than the sum of the two numbers diagonally above it in the previous row. What is the units digit of the sum of the $2023$ numbers in the $2023$rd row?

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/603e8ece698b5dc201f27d9da27bf217839dc0b197016a8b5852acd984fa0170.jpg]

solution_info.solution_info:
The sums of the entries in the first 6 rows equal 1, 2, 5, 12, 27, and 58. Note that these sums equal $2^{n}-n$ for $1 \leq n \leq 6$. That this formula is valid for arbitrary $n$ can be proved using mathematical induction, as follows. Let $s_{n}$ be the sum of the entries in row $n$ and assume the formula holds for row $n$, i.e., $s_{n}=2^{n}-n$. Each of the $(n-2)$ interior entries $k$ in row $n$ (other than the end 1s) contributes $2 k$ to $s_{n+1}$, and the plus 1 rule for generating the array contributes another $n-1$ to $s_{n+1}$. The end 1 s in row $n$ contribute 2 to $s_{n+1}$, and the end 1 s of row $n+1$ add another 2 to $s_{n+1}$. This gives

$s_{n+1}=2\left(s_{n}-2\right)+(n-1)+2+2=2\left(2^{n}-n-2\right)+n+3=2^{n+1}-(n+1)$
and the proof is complete. Thus the sum of the entries in the 2023rd row is $2^{2023}-2023$.

It remains to compute the units digit of $2^{2023}-2023$. Note that the units digits of successive powers of 2 form the sequence $2,4,8,6,2,4,8,6, \ldots$. Because 2023 leaves a remainder of 3 when divided by 4 , the units digit of $2^{2023}$ is 8 . The requested units digit is therefore $8-3=(\text{C})\boxed{5}$.

$\textbf{OR}$
Let $a_{n, k}$ be the $k$ th entry in the $n$th row of the array, and let $b_{n, k}=a_{n, k}+1$. Then

$\begin{aligned} b_{n, k} & =a_{n, k}+1 \\ & =\left(a_{n-1, k-1}+a_{n-1, k}+1\right)+1 \\ & =\left(a_{n-1, k-1}+1\right)+\left(a_{n-1, k}+1\right) \\ & =b_{n-1, k-1}+b_{n-1, k} \end{aligned}$
for $1 \leq k \leq n-1$. Because $b_{n, k}$ satisfies this Pascal Identity together with the conditions $b_{n, 0}=$ $b_{n, n}=2$, these values must be 2 times the binomial coefficients: $b_{n, k}=2\binom{n-1}{k}$. In other words, the resulting triangle is 2 times the ordinary Pascal Triangle.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/561f23b06cfaa3f375d9173386554b2a01405608112099bf19ce74b84bee938b.jpg]

Therefore the sum of the 2023 entries in row 2023 of this array is $2 \cdot 2^{2022}$, and the sum of the 2023 entries in row 2023 of the original array is $2 \cdot 2^{2022}-2023$, as above.

Note: The sequence whose $n$th term is $2^{n}-n$ arises in many different contexts; see A000325 in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences.

raw_content.title: If $A$ and $B$ are vertices of a polyhedron, define the distance $d(A, B)$ to be the minimum number of edges of the polyhedron one must traverse in order to connect $A$ and $B$. For example, if $\overline{A B}$ is an edge of the polyhedron, then $d(A, B)=1$, but if $\overline{A C}$ and $\overline{C B}$ are edges and $\overline{A B}$ is not an edge, then $d(A, B)=2$. Let $Q, R$, and $S$ be randomly chosen distinct vertices of a regular icosahedron (regular polyhedron made up of $20$ equilateral triangles). What is the probability that $d(Q, R)>d(R, S)$?

solution_info.solution_info:
One way to envision a regular icosahedron is with pentagonal pyramids on top and bottom, joined by a pentagonal antiprism. Let vertex $A$ be at the top, as illustrated.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/c8ebef9b2014715c6d8e60f8cffc411e8c07a9c753c26ae9b1929a6823f515a6.jpg]

There are five vertices on the base of the pyramid with apex $A$, so they are all at distance 1 from $A$. There are five vertices on the base of the pyramid with apex $B$, which are all at distance 1 from the previous five vertices, so they are at distance 2 from $A$. Finally, only vertex $B$ is at distance 3 from $A$. Thus from any vertex, there are 5 vertices at distance 1,5 at distance 2 , and 1 at distance 3 . Randomly select $Q, R$, and $S$ from the 12 vertices. Let $\mathbb{P}[E]$ denote the probability of event $E$, and let $\mathbb{P}[E \mid F]$ denote the probability of event $E$ given event $F$. By symmetry

$\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)>d(R, S)]=\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)<d(R, S)]$
so it suffices to compute $\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)=d(R, S)]$ and divide its complement by 2 to find $\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)>$ $d(R, S)]$. Note that $\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)=1]=\frac{5}{11}$ and

$\mathbb{P}[d(R, S)=1 \mid d(Q, R)=1]=\frac{4}{10}=\frac{2}{5},$
because vertex $Q$ is not available. Therefore

$\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)=d(R, S)=1]=\frac{5}{11} \cdot \frac{2}{5}=\frac{2}{11} .$
Because the number of vertices that are at distance 2 from $Q$ is also $5, \mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)=d(R, S)=2]$ is also $\frac{2}{11}$.\

Note that $d(Q, R)=d(R, S)=3$ is impossible, because $Q$ and $S$ are distinct. Therefore

$\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)>d(R, S)]=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{2}{11}-\frac{2}{11}\right)=(\text{A})\boxed{\frac{7}{22}} .$
$\textbf{OR}$
Use the same setting and notation as in the first solution. If $d(Q, R)=1$, then $d(Q, R) \ngtr d(R, S)$. If $d(Q, R)=3$, then $d(Q, R)>d(R, S)$, and this happens with probability $\frac{1}{11}$. If $d(Q, R)=2$, then $d(Q, R)>d(R, S)$ exactly when $d(R, S)=1$, which happens for 5 vertices of the remaining 10 from which to choose. Because $\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)=2]=\frac{5}{11}$,

$\mathbb{P}[d(R, S)=1 \mid d(Q, R)=2]=\frac{5}{10}=\frac{1}{2},$
so

$\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)>d(R, S) \text { and } d(Q, R)=2]=\frac{5}{11} \cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{5}{22} .$
The two ways found are mutually exclusive, so $\mathbb{P}[d(Q, R)>d(R, S)]=\frac{1}{11}+\frac{5}{22}=(\text{A})\boxed{\frac{7}{22}}$.

raw_content.title:
Let $f$ be the unique function defined on the positive integers such that

$\sum_{d \mid n} d \cdot f\left(\dfrac{n}{d}\right)=1$
for all positive integers $n$, where the sum is taken over all positive divisors of $n$. What is $f(2023)$?

solution_info.solution_info:
The number 1 has 1 divisor, so $1 \cdot f(1)=1$, and hence $f(1)=1$. If $n$ is a prime number, say $n=p$, then $n$ has 2 divisors, namely 1 and $p$, and so $1=1 \cdot f(p)+p \cdot f(1)=f(p)+p$, and hence $f(p)=1-p$ for all primes $p$. If $p$ is prime and $n=p^{2}$, then $n$ has 3 divisors, namely 1 , $p$, and $p^{2}$, so

$1=1 \cdot f\left(p^{2}\right)+p f(p)+p^{2} f(1)=f\left(p^{2}\right)+p(1-p)+p^{2}$
which says that $f\left(p^{2}\right)=1-p$. If $p$ and $q$ are distinct primes and $n=p q$, then $n$ has 4 divisors, and

$1=1 \cdot f(p q)+p f(q)+q f(p)+p q f(1)=f(p q)+p(1-q)+q(1-p)+p q$
so $f(p q)=(1-p)(1-q)$. If $p$ and $q$ are distinct primes, then $p q^{2}$ has 6 divisors, and

$\begin{aligned} 1 & =1 \cdot f\left(p q^{2}\right)+p f\left(q^{2}\right)+q f(p q)+p q f(q)+q^{2} f(p)+p q^{2} f(1) \\ & =f\left(p q^{2}\right)+p(1-q)+q(1-p)(1-q)+p q(1-q)+q^{2}(1-p)+p q^{2} \end{aligned}$
which gives $f\left(p q^{2}\right)=(1-p)(1-q)$. Because $2023=7 \cdot 17^{2}$, it follows that $f(2023)=$ $(-6)(-16)=(\text{B})\boxed{96}$.

raw_content.title:
How many ordered pairs of positive real numbers $(a, b)$ satisfy the equation

$(1+2 a)(2+2 b)(2 a+b)=32 a b?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Divide each side of the given equation by $a b$. The equation can then be expanded and regrouped as follows:

$\begin{aligned} (1+2 a)(2+2 b)\left(\frac{2}{b}+\frac{1}{a}\right) & =32 \\ (2+4 a+2 b+4 a b)\left(\frac{2}{b}+\frac{1}{a}\right) & =32 \\ \frac{4}{b}+\frac{8 a}{b}+4+8 a+\frac{2}{a}+4+\frac{2 b}{a}+4 b & =32 \\ 8+4\left(2 a+\frac{1}{2 a}\right)+4\left(b+\frac{1}{b}\right)+4\left(\frac{2 a}{b}+\frac{b}{2 a}\right) & =32 . \end{aligned}$
Recall that $x+\frac{1}{x} \geq 2$ for all positive real numbers $x$, with equality if and only if $x=1$. Therefore the left-hand side of this equation is bounded below by $8+8+8+8$, and the only solution occurs when $2 a=1$ and $b=1$.

$\textbf{OR}$
Applying the Arithmetic Mean-Geometric Mean Inequality gives the following statements:

$1+2 a=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+a+a \geq 4 \sqrt[4]{\frac{a^{2}}{4}}$; equality holds if and only if $a=\frac{1}{2}$;

$2+2 b=1+1+b+b \geq 4 \sqrt[4]{b^{2}}$; equality holds if and only if $b=1$;

$2 a+b=a+a+\frac{b}{2}+\frac{b}{2} \geq 4 \sqrt[4]{\frac{a^{2} b^{2}}{4}}$; equality holds if and only if $b=2 a$.

Multiplying the three inequalities above gives $(1+2 a)(2+2 b)(2 a+b) \geq 32 a b$, and equality holds if and only if $a=\frac{1}{2}$ and $b=1$.

raw_content.title: Let $K$ be the number of sequences $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$ such that $n$ is a positive integer less than or equal to $10$ , each $A_{i}$ is a subset of $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 10\}$, and $A_{i-1}$ is a subset of $A_{i}$ for each $i$ between $2$ and $n$, inclusive. For example, $\{\},\{5,7\},\{2,5,7\},\{2,5,7\},\{2,5,6,7,9\}$ is one such sequence, with $n=5$. What is the remainder when $K$ is divided by $10$?

solution_info.solution_info:
Such a sequence can be described by a value of $n$ together with a function $f$ from $\{1,2,3, \ldots, 10\}$ to $\{1,2, \ldots, n, n+1\}$ such that $f(j)$ is the least $i$ such that $j \in A_{i}$ if $j \in A_{n}$ and $f(j)=n+1$ if $j \notin A_{n}$. The number of such functions is $(n+1)^{10}$, because there are $n+1$ choices for where to send each element of the domain. Therefore $K=2^{10}+3^{10}+4^{10}+\cdots+11^{10}$. It remains to determine the remainders when each of the terms in this sum is divided by 10.

Powers of 2: The remainders of powers of 2 have the pattern $2,4,8,6,2,4,8,6,2,4$, so $2^{10}$ contributes 4 to the sum.

Powers of 3: The remainders of powers of 3 have the pattern $3,9,7,1,3,9,7,1,3,9$, so $3^{10}$ contributes 9 .

Powers of 4: The remainders of powers of 4 have the pattern $4,6,4,6,4,6,4,6,4,6$, so $4^{10}$ contributes 6 .

Powers of 5: All powers of 5 have remainder 5 .

Powers of 6: All powers of 6 have remainder 6 .

Powers of 7: The remainders of powers of 7 have the pattern $7,9,3,1,7,9,3,1,7,9$, so $7^{10}$ contributes 9 .

Powers of 8: The remainders of powers of 8 have the pattern $8,4,2,6,8,4,2,6,8,4$, so $8^{10}$ contributes 4 .

Powers of 9: The remainders of powers of 9 are alternately 9 and 1 , so that term contributes 1 .

Finally, $10^{10}$ contributes 0 and $11^{10}$ contributes 1 . Therefore the remainder when $K$ is divided by 10 is the same as the remainder when $4+9+6+5+6+9+4+1+0+1=45$ is divided by 10 , namely $(\text{C})\boxed{5}$ .

$\textbf{OR}$
As above, it suffices to compute the remainder when $2^{10}+3^{10}+4^{10}+\cdots+11^{10}$ is divided by 10 . Note that $m^{10} \equiv m^{2}(\bmod 10)$ for all $m$. Then modulo 10 ,\

$K=2^{10}+3^{10}+\cdots+11^{10} \equiv 2^{2}+3^{2}+\cdots+11^{2}=\frac{11 \cdot(11+1) \cdot(2 \cdot 11+1)}{6}-1=505 \equiv(\text{C})\boxed{5}$.

Note: In fact, $K=40,851,766,525$.

raw_content.title:
There is a unique sequence of integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots, a_{2023}$ such that

$\tan 2023 x=\dfrac{a_{1} \tan x+a_{3} \tan ^{3} x+a_{5} \tan ^{5} x+\cdots+a_{2023} \tan ^{2023} x}{1+a_{2} \tan ^{2} x+a_{4} \tan ^{4} x+\cdots+a_{2022} \tan ^{2022} x}$
whenever $\tan 2023 x$ is defined. What is $a_{2023}$?

solution_info.solution_info:
By de Moivre's Formula and the Binomial Theorem,

$\begin{aligned} \cos n x+i \sin n x= & (\cos x+i \sin x)^{n} \\ = & \cos ^{n} x \end{aligned}+i\binom{n}{1} \cos ^{n-1} x \cdot \sin x+i^{2}\binom{n}{2} \cos ^{n-2} x \cdot \sin ^{2} x .$
By equating the real and imaginary parts of the respective sides above, it follows that for odd $n$,

$\cos n x=\cos ^{n} x-\binom{n}{2} \cos ^{n-2} x \cdot \sin ^{2} x+\binom{n}{4} \cos ^{n-4} x \cdot \sin ^{4} x-\cdots \pm\binom{ n}{n-1} \cos x \cdot \sin ^{n-1} x$
$=C_{n}(\cos x, \sin x)$
and

$\begin{aligned} \sin n x & =\binom{n}{1} \cos ^{n-1} x \cdot \sin x-\binom{n}{3} \cos ^{n-3} x \cdot \sin ^{3} x+\cdots \pm \sin ^{n} x \\ & =S_{n}(\cos x, \sin x), \end{aligned}$
where $C_{n}(u, v)$ and $S_{n}(u, v)$ are homogeneous polynomials of degree $n$. (A homogeneous polynomial is a polynomial for which all terms have the same total degree.) Hence

$\tan n x=\frac{S_{n}(\cos x, \sin x)}{C_{n}(\cos x, \sin x)} .$
By dividing the numerator and denominator above by $\cos ^{n} x$, it follows that

$\tan n x=\frac{S_{n}(1, \tan x)}{C_{n}(1, \tan x)} .$
The general term in $S_{n}(u, v)$ has the form

$(-1)^{k}\binom{n}{2 k+1} u^{n-2 k-1} v^{2 k+1},$
so with $n=2023$, the last term occurs when $k=1011$. Hence the last term of $S_{n}(1, \tan x)$ is $-1\binom{2023}{2023} v^{2023}$, and thus $a_{2023}=(\text{C})\boxed{-1}$.

solution_info.solution_info:

When the roots of the polynomial

$P(x)=(x-1)^{1}(x-2)^{2}(x-3)^{3} \cdots(x-10)^{10}$
are removed from the real number line, what remains is the union of $11$ disjoint open intervals. On how many of these intervals is $P(x)$ positive?

solution_info.solution_info:
Note that the function $P(x)>0$ for $x>10$. Moving right to left along the real number line, $P(x)$ changes sign precisely when passing through a root of odd multiplicity. This means that the function changes sign as $x$ passes through $9,7,5,3$, and 1 , and its value is 0 at $10,8,6,4$, and 2 as well. Therefore $P(x)>0$ on the intervals $(10, \infty),(9,10),(6,7),(5,6),(2,3)$, and $(1,2)$, a total of $(\text{C})\boxed{6}$ intervals.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/8dbcaadb05983cc17913d15a495d387a4e7794a9ab5b63ba937170d194ae4b5e.jpg]

$\textbf{OR}$
Perfect square factors are always nonnegative, so they can be removed without changing the signs. Therefore, for any $x$ with $P(x) \neq 0$, the polynomial

$Q(x)=(x-1)(x-3)(x-5)(x-7)(x-9)$
will have the same sign as $P(x)$. Now $Q(x)$ is positive on the following intervals: $(1,2)$ and $(2,3)$ (where four of the factors are negative), $(5,6)$ and $(6,7)$ (where two of the factors are negative), and $(9,10)$ and $(10, \infty)$ (where all the factors are positive). This gives a total of $(\text{C})\boxed{6}$ intervals on which $Q(x)>0$. On the other 5 intervals there are an odd number of negative factors, so $Q(x)$, and therefore $P(x)$ as well, is negative.

raw_content.title:
For how many integers $n$ does the expression

$\sqrt{\frac{\log \left(n^{2}\right)-(\log n)^{2}}{\log n-3}}$
represent a real number, where log denotes the base $10$ logarithm?

solution_info.solution_info:
First note that the fraction under the square root will equal 0 when $n=1$. There are now 2 cases to consider: Either $\log n>3$ or $\log n<3$. In the first case, $\log n>3$ gives $n>1000$, so the numerator $\log \left(n^{2}\right)-(\log n)^{2}=2 \log n-(\log n)^{2}<0$ because $2 \log n<(\log n)^{2}$ whenever $\log n>2$. Thus the fraction under the square root will be negative and there are no solutions in this case.

For the second case, $\log n<3$, so $n<1000$. The fraction under the square root will be nonnegative provided $\log \left(n^{2}\right)-(\log n)^{2} \leq 0$. This will occur when $\log n \geq 2$, i.e., when $n \geq 100$. Thus the given expression will evaluate to a real number for any integer $n$ in the range $100 \leq n<1000$. Together with the $n=1$ solution, this gives a total of $(\text{E})\boxed{901}$ integers for which the expression evaluates to a real number.

$\textbf{OR}$
If the expression represents a real number, then $\log n$ is defined, so $n>0$. Because $n$ is an integer, $n>0$ implies $n \geq 1$. Let $m=\log n \geq \log 1=0$. The fraction under the square root can be expressed as

$\frac{2 m-m^{2}}{m-3}=\frac{m(2-m)}{m-3}$
This expression is meaningful and nonnegative when $m=0$ or $2 \leq m<3$, as shown in the table below. If $m=0$, then $n=1$. When $2 \leq m<3$, it follows that $100 \leq n<1000$ and hence another 900 integral values of $n$ make the expression represent a real number. This gives a total of $1+900=(\text{E})\boxed{901}$ possible values of $n$.

$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} & m & 2-m & m-3 & \frac{m(2-m)}{m-3} \\ \hline m=0 & 0 & + & - & 0 \\ \hline 0<m<2 & + & + & - & - \\ \hline m=2 & + & 0 & - & 0 \\ \hline 2<m<3 & - & - & - & + \\ \hline m=3 & + & - & 0 & undefined \\ \hline m>3 & + & - & + & - \\ \hline \end{array}$

raw_content.title: How many nonempty subsets $B$ of $\{0,1,2,3, \ldots, 12\}$ have the property that the number of elements in $B$ is equal to the least element of $B$ ? For example, $B=\{4,6,8,11\}$ satisfies the condition.

solution_info.solution_info:
Any nonempty subset satisfying this property with minimum value $k$ must contain $k-1$ elements greater than $k$. This implies that $1 \leq k \leq 6$, and there are $\binom{12-k}{k-1}$ such subsets. The total number of subsets with the required property is therefore

$\binom{6}{5}+\binom{7}{4}+\binom{8}{3}+\binom{9}{2}+\binom{10}{1}+\binom{11}{0}=6+35+56+36+10+1=(\text{D})\boxed{144} .$
Note: This problem illustrates an identity relating the sum of the elements on a "shallow" diagonal in Pascal's triangle to the Fibonacci numbers.

In rectangular coordinates, the equations of the circles are $(x-4)^{2}+y^{2}=4^{2}$ and $x^{2}+(y-10)^{2}=10^{2}$, respectively. Subtracting the two equations and simplifying yields $y=\frac{2}{5} x$. Any point lying on both circles must satisfy this equation, which must therefore be the equation of the line through the two points of intersection. The requested slope is therefore $(\text{E})\boxed{\frac{2}{5}}$.

$\textbf{OR}$
Let $A(4,0)$ and $C(0,10)$ be the centers of the two circles, and let $O$ and $B$ be their intersection points. Because $C O=C B$ and $A O=A B$, the diagonals of kite $O A B C$ are perpendicular. raw_content.title:
For complex numbers $u=a+b i$ and $v=c+d i$ (where $i=\sqrt{-1}$ ), define the binary operation

$u \otimes v=a c+b d i$
Suppose $z$ is a complex number such that $z \otimes z=z^{2}+40$. What is $|z|$?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $z=a+b i$. Then $z \otimes z=a^{2}+b^{2} i$ and $z^{2}=\left(a^{2}-b^{2}\right)+2 a b i$, so the original equation is equivalent to

$a^{2}+b^{2} i=\left(a^{2}-b^{2}+40\right)+2 a b i$
Setting the real parts of both sides equal gives $b^{2}=40$, so $b= \pm 2 \sqrt{10}$. Setting the imaginary parts of both sides equal yields $a=\frac{b}{2}= \pm \sqrt{10}$. Then

$|z|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\sqrt{10+40}=(\text{E})\boxed{5 \sqrt{2}}$

raw_content.title: A rectangular box $\mathcal{P}$ has distinct edge lengths $a, b$, and $c$. The sum of the lengths of all $12$ edges of $\mathcal{P}$ is $13$ the sum of the areas of all $6$ faces of $\mathcal{P}$ is $11 / 2$, and the volume of $\mathcal{P}$ is $1 / 2$. What is the length of the longest interior diagonal connecting two vertices of $\mathcal{P}$?

solution_info.solution_info:
The longest diagonal passes through the interior of the box, connecting opposite vertices; its length is $\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}$. Because $4 a+4 b+4 c=13$ and $2 a b+2 b c+2 a c=\frac{11}{2}$, it follows that

$\left(\frac{13}{4}\right)^{2}=(a+b+c)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2 a b+2 b c+2 a c=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+\frac{11}{2}$
Therefore

$a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=\left(\frac{13}{4}\right)^{2}-\frac{11}{2}=\frac{81}{16}$
The longest diagonal has length $\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}=(\text{D})\boxed{\frac{9}{4}}$.

Note: Such a box $\mathcal{P}$ exists with edge lengths $\frac{1}{4}, 1$, and 2 . The volume is not needed to solve this problem.

raw_content.title: For how many ordered pairs $(a, b)$ of integers does the polynomial $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+6$ have $3$ distinct integer roots?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $r, s$, and $t$ be the roots of $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+6$. Then

$x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+6=(x-r)(x-s)(x-t)=x^{3}-(r+s+t) x^{2}+(r s+s t+t r) x-r s t$
so $r s t=-6, r+s+t=-a$, and $r s+s t+t r=b$. Because $r, s$, and $t$ are distinct integers and $r s t=-6$, the possible roots $\{r, s, t\}$ are the sets $\{-1,1,6\},\{-1,2,3\},\{1,-2,3\},\{1,2,-3\}$, and $\{-1,-2,-3\}$. The corresponding ordered pairs $(a, b)$ are $(-6,-1),(-4,1),(-2,-5),(0,-7)$, and $(6,11)$, respectively. This gives $(\text{A})\boxed{5}$ possible ordered pairs $(a, b)$.

raw_content.title:
Suppose that $a, b$, and $c$ are positive integers such that

$\frac{a}{14}+\frac{b}{15}=\frac{c}{210}$

Which of the following statements are necessarily true?

$I$. If $\operatorname{gcd}(a,14)=1$ or $\operatorname{gcd}(b,15)=1$ or both, then $\operatorname{gcd}(c,210)=1$.

$II$. If $\operatorname{gcd}(c,210)=1$, then $\operatorname{gcd}(a,14)=1$ or $\operatorname{gcd}(b,15)=1$ or both.

$III$. $\operatorname{gcd}(c,210)=1$ if and only if $\operatorname{gcd}(a,14)=1$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(b,15)=1$.

solution_info.solution_info:
Note that 14 and 15 are relatively prime and $210=14 \cdot 15$. Let $q$ and $r$ be two relatively prime positive integers (such as 14 and 15). The equation $\frac{a}{q}+\frac{b}{r}=\frac{c}{q r}$ is equivalent to $a r+b q=c$. Hence

$\operatorname{gcd}(c, q)=\operatorname{gcd}(a r+b q, q)=\operatorname{gcd}(a r, q)=\operatorname{gcd}(a, q)$
Similarly, $\operatorname{gcd}(c, r)=\operatorname{gcd}(b, r)$. Also, $\operatorname{gcd}(c, q r)=1$ if and only if $\operatorname{gcd}(c, q)=1$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(c, r)=1$. Therefore Statement III is true, and that statement logically implies Statement II. To see that Statement I might be false, let $a=1, b=3$, and $c=57$; then the hypothesis is true but the conclusion is false. Thus Statements $(\text{E})\boxed{II and III}$ are the only ones that are necessarily true.

raw_content.title: In the state of Coinland, coins have values of $6,10$ and $15$ cents. Suppose $x$ is the value in cents of the most expensive item in Coinland that cannot be purchased using these coins with exact change. What is the sum of the digits of $x$?

solution_info.solution_info:
The problem is asking for the sum of the digits of the greatest integer $x$ that cannot be written in the form $6 a+10 b+15 c$, where $a, b$, and $c$ are nonnegative integers.. If $c=0$, then $6 a+10 b+15 c$ is a multiple of 2 . If $b=0$, then $6 a+10 b+15 c$ is a multiple of 3 . If $a=0$, then $6 a+10 b+15 c$ is a multiple of 5 . If none of $a, b$, or $c$ equals 0 , then $6 a+10 b+15 c \geq 6+10+15=31$. Therefore prime numbers less than 31 cannot be written in the required form. In particular, 29 cannot be written in this form.

To show that 29 is the greatest positive integer that cannot be written as such a sum, observe that the following six consecutive integers can be written in this way.

$\begin{aligned} & 30=15+15 \\ & 31=6+10+15 \\ & 32=6+6+10+10 \\ & 33=6+6+6+15 \\ & 34=6+6+6+6+10 \\ & 35=10+10+15 \end{aligned}$
Because additional 6 s can be added to each of these sums, it follows that all positive integers greater than 29 can be written in the required form. Therefore the most expensive item in Coinland that cannot be purchased using coins of the given denominations has value $x=29$, and the requested digit sum is $2+9=(\text{D})\boxed{11}$.

raw_content.title: The three side lengths of a triangle are in arithmetic progression with shortest side of length $6$ One of the interior angles measures $120^{\circ}$. What is the area of the triangle?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $a$ and $d$ be positive real numbers such that the side lengths are $a-d$, $a$, and $a+d$. Then the longest side, that of length $a+d$, must be opposite the $120^{\circ}$ angle. By the Law of Cosines,

$(a+d)^{2}=a^{2}+(a-d)^{2}-2 a(a-d) \cos 120^{\circ} .$
Simplifying yields $2 a^{2}-5 a d=0$, so $a(2 a-5 d)=0$ and $d=\frac{2}{5} a$. Therefore the three sides have lengths $\frac{3}{5} a, a, \frac{7}{5} a$. Because the shortest side has length 6 , the three side lengths are $6,10,14$.\

The area of the triangle is

$\frac{1}{2} \cdot 6 \cdot 10 \cdot \sin 120^{\circ}=30 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=(\text{E})\boxed{15 \sqrt{3}} .$
Alternatively, one can use Heron's Formula with $s=\frac{6+10+14}{2}=15$ to find the area.

Note: A triple of integers that are the side lengths of a triangle with exactly one $60^{\circ}$ angle is called an Eisenstein triple, similar to a Pythagorean triple for a triangle with a $90^{\circ}$ angle. Some examples of such triples are $(3,7,8)$ and $(8,13,15)$. Similarly, there are other triangles with integer side lengths and a $120^{\circ}$ angle, such as $(7,8,13)$ and $(5,16,19)$.

raw_content.title: Last academic year Yolanda and Zelda took different courses that did not necessarily administer the same number of quizzes during each of the two semesters. Yolanda's average on all the quizzes she took during the first semester was $3$ points higher than Zelda's average on all the quizzes she took during the first semester. Yolanda's average on all the quizzes she took during the second semester was $18$ points higher than her average for the first semester and was again $3$ points higher than Zelda's average on all the quizzes Zelda took during her second semester. Which one of the following statements cannot possibly be true?
raw_content.option_a: Yolanda's quiz average for the academic year was $22$ points higher than Zelda's.
raw_content.option_b: Zelda's quiz average for the academic year was higher than Yolanda's.
raw_content.option_c: Yolanda's quiz average for the academic year was $3$ points higher than Zelda's.
raw_content.option_d: Zelda's quiz average for the academic year equaled Yolanda's.
raw_content.option_e: If Zelda had scored $3$ points higher on each quiz she took, then she would have had the same average for the academic year as Yolanda.

solution_info.solution_info:
To see that choice (C) might be true, observe that Yolanda's average on quizzes for the whole academic year would have been 3 points higher than Zelda's if the number of quizzes in each course was the same each semester. And if all courses have the same number of quizzes, the same argument shows that choice ( $\mathbf{E}$ ) is also possible.

While counterintuitive, choice (B) could be true; this is an example of Simpson's Paradox. Indeed, suppose Yolanda's average was $X$ during her first semester. Then Yolanda's average was $X+18$ her second semester and Zelda's averages were $X-3$ and $X+15$ her two semesters. Suppose Yolanda took 8 quizzes her first semester and 2 quizzes her second semester, while Zelda took 2 quizzes her first semester and 8 quizzes her second semester. Then Yolanda's average for the whole academic year would have been

$\frac{8 X+2(X+18)}{8+2}=X+3.6$
and Zelda's would have been

$\frac{2(X-3)+8(X+15)}{2+8}=X+11.4$
so Zelda would have had the better average for the whole academic year. Choice (D) could be true in much the same way. Again suppose Yolanda took 8 quizzes her first semester and 2 quizzes her second semester, and suppose Zelda took $a$ quizzes her first semester and $b$ quizzes her second semester. Then their averages would both have been $X+3.6$ if and only if

$\frac{a(X-3)+b(X+15)}{a+b}=X+3.6 .$
This equation is equivalent to $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{11.4}{6.6}$, which will be true if $a=114$ and $b=66$ (or $a=19$ and $b=11$ ).

This leaves choice (A) as the only possible answer to this problem. To see that Yolanda's average on quizzes for the whole academic year cannot have been 22 points higher than Zelda's, use the notation as above and observe that Yolanda's average for the whole academic year must have been between $X$ and $X+18$ and Zelda's must have been between $X-3$ and $X+15$. The greatest possible difference in their averages for the academic year is therefore less than $(X+18)-(X-3)=21$ points and cannot be 22 points.

raw_content.title: Cyrus the frog sits on a flat surface. He jumps, landing $2$ feet away. He then chooses a direction at random and again jumps $2$ feet. What is the probability that after the second jump Cyrus lands within $1$ foot of his starting position?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $A$ be the starting position, and let $B$ be Cyrus's position after the first jump. Let $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ be the points at which the circle of radius 2 centered at $B$ (which consists of all of Cyrus's possible positions after the second jump) intersects the circle of radius 1 centered at $A$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/000911b594c628207249411eb5dea06e44e26007dd2a3d0b9e06566452af293c.jpg]

Cyrus will land within 1 foot of his starting position after the second jump if and only if he lands on minor arc $\widehat{C_{1} C_{2}}$. Therefore the requested probability is the fraction of the perimeter of the circle occupied by this arc. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $\overline{A C_{1}}$. Because $\triangle A B C_{1}$ is isosceles, $\angle B M C_{1}$ is a right angle.

Then

$\sin \left(\angle M B C_{1}\right)=\frac{M C_{1}}{B C_{1}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot 1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}$
Note that $\angle M B C_{1}=\frac{1}{4} \cdot \angle C_{1} B C_{2}$. The fraction of the perimeter occupied by minor arc $\widehat{C_{1} C_{2}}$ and the requested probability is therefore

$\frac{4 \arcsin \frac{1}{4}}{2 \pi}=(\text{E})\boxed{\frac{2 \arcsin \frac{1}{4}}{\pi}}$
This value is about 0.161 , slightly less than $\frac{1}{6}$.

The bug wants to crawl to the honey, but it must stay on the surface of the lampshade. What is the length in inches of its shortest path to the honey?

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/1998cd5525a8ae1b1f7627dda6ed8ad09c73197e99cdb32b10420ed10af00d85.jpg]

solution_info.solution_info:
The circumference of the bottom of the cone is $12 \pi$, the height of the (full) cone is $6 \sqrt{3}$, and the slant height of the cone is 12 .

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/902120d42a81df8e08855be555b96f8cea2c5d27faa5fcbc455bed3d9449ad0d.jpg]

When the frustum is slit along the slant height and rolled out (into a sector of an annulus), the outer radius will be 12 and the arc length will be $12 \pi$, making the measure of the arc $180^{\circ}$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/6ea94e71cf6800c130b13f2e73c634d41e5de6d77b3ed91bbe2b1a4a7cfb2b2f.jpg]

Refer to the unrolled figure. The bug wants to crawl from point $B$ to point $H$. Note that because $H$ is at the top of the inner semicircle and $B$ is to the right of its center, $\overline{B H}$ passes through the interior of the semicircle and thus does not remain on the surface of the lampshade, as required. semicircle to $H$. The inside radius is 6 , so $\triangle B C D$ is a $30-60-90^{\circ}$ right triangle and $B D=6 \sqrt{3}$. Because $\overline{H C} \perp \overline{B C}$ and $\angle B C D=60^{\circ}$, it follows that $\angle H C D=30^{\circ}$. Therefore the length of $\widehat{D H}$ is

raw_content.title:
A real-valued function $f$ has the property that for all real numbers $a$ and $b$,

$f(a+b)+f(a-b)=2 f(a) f(b)$

Which one of the following cannot be the value of $f(1)$?

solution_info.solution_info:
First note that if $f(x)=0$ for all $x$, then the defining identity is met, and $f(1)=0$, eliminating option (A). Now assume that $f$ is not identically zero. Setting $b=0$ and choosing $a$ so that $f(a) \neq 0$, the identity reduces to $f(a)+f(a)=2 f(a) f(0)$, yielding $f(0)=1$. Setting $a=b=\frac{1}{2}$ and using $f(0)=1$ gives $f(1)+1=2 f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$. If $f(1)=-2$, then $-2+1=$ $2\left[f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right]^{2}$, which is impossible. So $f(1)$ cannot equal $(\text{E})\boxed{-2}$ , and the correct answer is (E).

For completeness, it remains to show why options (C), (B) and (D) are attainable as $f(1)$. Note that the cosine function satisfies the defining identity, as does the hyperbolic cosine function, and more generally so do $\cos (k x)$ and $\cosh (k x)$. Letting $k$ equal $\pi, \frac{\pi}{2}$, and 0 in $\cos (k x)$, respectively, shows that options (C), (A), and $(\mathbf{B})$ are possible values of $f(1)$. The range of the continuous function $f(x)=\cosh (k x)$ is the interval $[1, \infty)$, which includes 2 . Therefore there must be a value of $k$ that makes $f(1)=2$, eliminating option (D).

Note: While not required for this problem, it is possible to determine a specific $x$ satisfying $\cosh x=$ 2. Observe that

$\begin{aligned} \cosh (\ln (2+\sqrt{3})) & =\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left(e^{\ln (2+\sqrt{3})}+e^{-\ln (2+\sqrt{3})}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left(2+\sqrt{3}+\frac{1}{(2+\sqrt{3})}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \cdot\left(2+\sqrt{3}+\frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{4-3}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \cdot(2+\sqrt{3}+2-\sqrt{3})=2 \end{aligned}$
so $f(1)=2$ when $f(x)=\cosh ((\ln (2+\sqrt{3})) x)$.

raw_content.title: When a standard $6$-sided die is rolled $n$ times, the product of the $n$ numbers rolled can be any of $936$ possible values. What is $n$?

solution_info.solution_info:
The product of the results of the rolls takes the form $2^{a} 3^{b} 5^{c}$, and every roll contributes at most two prime factors to the product. No roll contributes more than one factor of 5 , so $0 \leq c \leq n$.

No roll contributes more than one factor of 3 , and no roll can contribute both a 3 and a 5 , so $0 \leq b \leq$ $n-c$. No roll contributes more than two factors of 2 , no roll that contributes a 3 can contribute more than one factor of 2 , and no roll can contribute both a 2 and a 5 , so $0 \leq a \leq 2 n-b-2 c$. Each ordered triple $(a, b, c)$ determines a different product, so the number of possible products is

$\begin{aligned} \sum_{c=0}^{n} \sum_{b=0}^{n-c}(2 n-b-2 c+1) & =\sum_{c=0}^{n}\left(\sum_{b=0}^{n-c}(2 n-2 c+1)-\sum_{b=0}^{n-c} b\right) \\ & =\sum_{c=0}^{n}\left((2(n-c)+1)(n-c+1)-\frac{1}{2}(n-c)(n-c+1)\right) \\ & =\sum_{c=0}^{n}\left((2 c+1)(c+1)-\frac{1}{2} c(c+1)\right) \\ & =\sum_{c=0}^{n}\left(\frac{3}{2} c^{2}+\frac{5}{2} c+1\right) \\ & =\frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}+\frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2}+(n+1) \\ & =\frac{(n+1)^{2}(n+2)}{2} \end{aligned}$
Note that $936=\frac{12^{2} \cdot 13}{2}$, so $n=(\text{A})\boxed{11}$.

raw_content.title:
Suppose that $a, b, c$, and $d$ are positive integers satisfying all of the following relations.

$a b c d =2^{6} \cdot 3^{9} \cdot 5^{7}$
$\operatorname{lcm}(a, b) =2^{3} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5^{3}$
$\operatorname{lcm}(a, c) =2^{3} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{3}$
$\operatorname{lcm}(a, d) =2^{3} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{3}$
$\operatorname{lcm}(b, c) =2^{1} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{2}$
$\operatorname{lcm}(b, d) =2^{2} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{2}$
$\operatorname{lcm}(c, d) =2^{2} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{2}$
What is $\operatorname{gcd}(a, b, c, d)$?

solution_info.solution_info:
Because $\operatorname{lcm}(b, c)$ contains just 1 factor of 2 , neither $b$ nor $c$ is divisible by $2^{2}$. However, $\operatorname{lcm}(b, d)$ contains 2 factors of 2 , and $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b)$ contains 3 factors, so $d$ is divisible by $2^{2}$, and $a$ is divisible by $2^{3}$. Because the product $a b c d$ contains 6 factors of 2 , it follows that one of $b$ or $c$ is divisible by 2 , and the other is not. Therefore $\operatorname{gcd}(a, b, c, d)$ is not divisible by 2.

Because $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b)$ contains just 2 factors of 3 , at least one of $a$ and $b$ is divisible by $3^{2}$, but neither is divisible by $3^{3}$. However, both $\operatorname{lcm}(a, c)$ and $\operatorname{lcm}(a, d)$ contain 3 factors of 3 , so both $c$ and $d$ are divisible by $3^{3}$. Because the product $a b c d$ contains 9 factors of 3, it follows that one of $a$ or $b$ is divisible by $3^{2}$, and the other is divisible by 3 but not by $3^{2}$. Therefore $\operatorname{gcd}(a, b, c, d)$ is divisible by 3 but not by $3^{2}$.

Because $1 \mathrm{~cm}(b, c), \operatorname{lcm}(b, d)$, and $\operatorname{lcm}(c, d)$ each contain just 2 factors of 5, none of $b, c$, or $d$ is divisible by $5^{3}$, but at least two of them are divisible by $5^{2}$. However, $\operatorname{lcm}(a, b)$ contains 3 factors of 5 , so $a$ is divisible by $5^{3}$. Because $a b c d$ contains 7 factors of 5 , it follows that two of $b, c$, and $d$ are divisible by $5^{2}$, and the other is not divisible by 5 . Therefore $\operatorname{gcd}(a, b, c, d)$ is not divisible by 5 .

Because $\operatorname{gcd}(a, b, c, d)$ cannot contain any prime factors other than 2,3 , or 5 , it follows that $\operatorname{gcd}(a, b, c, d)=(\text{C})\boxed{3}$.

$\textbf{OR}$
Let $\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right]$ denote the least common multiple of $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ and $\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\right)$ denote their greatest common divisor. Because $[a, b, c]=[[a, b],[b, c]]$ and $[a, b, c, d]=[[a, b],[c, d]]$ the following relations are satisfied.

$\begin{aligned} {[a, b, c] } & =2^{3} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{3} \\ {[b, c, d] } & =2^{2} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{3} \\ {[c, d, a] } & =2^{3} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{3} \\ {[d, a, b] } & =2^{3} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{3} \\ {[a, b, c, d] } & =2^{3} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 5^{3} \end{aligned}$
It now remains to appeal to the identity

$(a, b, c, d)=\frac{a b c d[a, b, c][b, c, d][c, d, a][d, a, b]}{[a, b][a, c][a, d][b, c][b, d][c, d][a, b, c, d]}$
This identity is a consequence of the identity

$\begin{aligned} & \min (\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta)=\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta \\ & \quad-(\max (\alpha, \beta)+\max (\alpha, \gamma)+\max (\alpha, \delta)+\max (\beta, \gamma)+\max (\beta, \delta)+\max (\gamma, \delta)) \\ & \quad+(\max (\alpha, \beta, \gamma)+\max (\beta, \gamma, \delta)+\max (\gamma, \delta, \alpha)+\max (\delta, \alpha, \beta)) \\ & \quad-\max (\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta) \end{aligned}$
To prove this identity, observe that the variables are treated symmetrically, so that one may assume that $\alpha \geq \beta \geq \gamma \geq \delta$. Then the above asserts that

$\delta=\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta-(\alpha+\alpha+\alpha+\beta+\beta+\gamma)+(\alpha+\beta+\alpha+\alpha)-\alpha$
and this can be verified by simplifying. Applying the identity to the given values gives $(a, b, c, d)=3$.\

Note: Here are several comments:

The pairwise lcm's determine all lcm's of $k$-tuples for any $k$, because

$\left[a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k}\right]=\left[\left[a_{1}, a_{2}\right],\left[a_{2}, a_{3}\right], \ldots,\left[a_{k-1}, a_{k}\right]\right]$

Because the gcd is computed easily by the Euclidean Algorithm, it is more common to express an lcm in terms of gcd's. The formula

$[a, b, c]=\frac{a b c(a, b, c)}{(a, b)(b, c)(c, a)}$
occurs in some texts in elementary number theory, but only very rarely.

If $A, B, C, D$ are sets and $I_{A}, I_{B}, I_{C}, I_{D}$ are their indicator functions, then $\max \left(I_{A}, I_{B}\right)=I_{A \cup B}$ and $\min \left(I_{A}, I_{B}\right)=I_{A \cap B}$. When $\alpha, \ldots, \delta$ are taken to be these indicator functions in the identity above, it becomes Euler's Inclusion-Exclusion principle. When the same substitution is made in the corresponding identity found in the second solution, an expression is obtained for the intersection of several sets in terms of the unions of various subcollections. This is the set-theoretic dual of the Inclusion-Exclusion Principle.

raw_content.title: A regular pentagon with area $1+\sqrt{5}$ is printed on paper and cut out. All five vertices are folded to the center of the pentagon, creating a smaller pentagon. What is the area of the new pentagon?

solution_info.solution_info:
The folds are the perpendicular bisectors of the segments connecting the vertices of the pentagon to its center. Let $C$ be the center of the pentagon, let $G, A$, and $F$ be three consecutive vertices in order, let $D$ be the intersection of the fold lines for vertices $A$ and $F$, let $B$ be the intersection of the fold lines for vertices $A$ and $G$, and let $E$ be the other intersection of fold lines on the fold line for $F$. Draw quadrilaterals $A B C D$ and $A B E F$, as shown.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/2611f019794111bf20d4947dfaf5a77463c267b8a6e4a41ad3b746f7aaf7b63a.jpg]

Let $S$ be the area of the small pentagon. Because the two pentagons are similar, the ratio of their areas is the square of the ratio of their side lengths. Therefore

$\frac{S}{1+\sqrt{5}}=\left(\frac{B D}{A F}\right)^{2}$
By symmetry, $A B C D$ must be a rhombus, and $\overline{A C}$ bisects $\angle B A D$ (and $\angle G A F$ ). Then

$\begin{gathered} \angle B A D=\angle B C D=\frac{360^{\circ}}{5}=72^{\circ} \\ \text { so } \angle B A C=\frac{72^{\circ}}{2}=36^{\circ} . \text { Also, } \angle G A F=\frac{3 \cdot 180^{\circ}}{5}=108^{\circ} \text {, so } \angle C A F=\frac{108^{\circ}}{2}=54^{\circ} . \text { Lastly, } \\ \angle B A F=\angle B A C+\angle C A F=36^{\circ}+54^{\circ}=90^{\circ} . \end{gathered}$
Therefore quadrilateral $A B E F$ is a rectangle and $B E=A F$. It is known (and proved below) that the ratio of a diagonal of a regular pentagon to its side is $\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ ( $\varphi$, the golden ratio). Therefore

$\frac{B D}{A F}=\frac{B D}{B E}=\frac{1}{\varphi}=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{5}},$
and

$\frac{S}{1+\sqrt{5}}=\left(\frac{B D}{A F}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{5}}\right)^{2} .$
The requested area is $S=\frac{2^{2}}{1+\sqrt{5}}=(\text{B})\boxed{\sqrt{5}-1}$.

To prove that the diagonal to side ratio for a regular pentagon equals $\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$, let regular pentagon PQRST have sides of length 1 and diagonals of length $d$, and let $U$ be the point of intersection of the line segments $\overline{P R}$ and $\overline{Q T}$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/09bd4643a727cce3cb87bca87d3e6e29dd5b48e6d6dd2587dd090d0819e33496.jpg]

Because each diagonal is parallel to a side, parallelogram TURS is formed with sides of length 1, leaving segments $\overline{P U}$ and $\overline{Q U}$ to have length $d-1$. Because $P Q R T$ is a trapezoid, $\triangle R T U$ and $\triangle P Q U$ are similar, and $\frac{d}{1}=\frac{1}{d-1}$. This implies that $d^{2}-d-1=0$, and the quadratic formula gives the positive solution $d=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}=\varphi$.

$\textbf{OR}$
Inscribe the regular pentagon in a circle of radius $r$. Let $A$ be the center of the circle, let $C$ be a vertex of the pentagon, and let $B$ be the midpoint of the minor arc from $C$ to one of the vertices adjacent to $C$. Let $D$ be the intersection of the bisector of $\angle A B C$ with $\overline{A C}$. Let $E$ be the midpoint of $\overline{A B}$, and let $F$ be the intersection of $\overline{A B}$ with the pentagon. Note that $A F$ is the center-to-side distance of the pentagon. See the figure.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/c841b8aeab11294fa5edf5ceae0a4d1e7f9cdd5ec8dedc9cf5cc978af28df17d.jpg]

The linear dimensions are reduced by the factor $f=\frac{r}{2 \cdot A F}$, and the area is reduced by the factor $f^{2}$. The scale factor $f$ can be evaluated using similar triangles. Triangle $\triangle A B C$ is isosceles with angles $36^{\circ}, 72^{\circ}, 72^{\circ}$ and sides $A B=A C=r$. Segment $\overline{B D}$ bisects $\angle A B C$ creating isosceles triangles $\triangle A B D$ with two $36^{\circ}$ angles and $\triangle B D C$ with two $72^{\circ}$ angles. Choose units so that $1=B C=B D=A D$. Notice that $\triangle B D C \sim \triangle A B C$ and is smaller by a factor of $r$. Because $A D+D C=A C$, it follows that $1+\frac{1}{r}=r$. Because $r>1$, this simplifies to $r=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$. Now

$f=\frac{A C}{2 \cdot A F}=\frac{A D}{2 \cdot A E}=\frac{1}{r}=\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{5}} .$
The area of the smaller pentagon is

$f^{2}(1+\sqrt{5})=\frac{4(1+\sqrt{5})}{(1+\sqrt{5})^{2}}=(\text{B})\boxed{\sqrt{5}-1}$

raw_content.title: What is the value of $101 \cdot 9,901-99 \cdot 10,101?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Write the difference as

$(100+1) \cdot(9900+1)-99 \cdot(10,000+100+1) .$
Applying the distributive property gives

$(990,000+9,900+100+1)-(990,000+9,900+99)=100+1-99=(\text{A})\boxed{2} .$
$\textbf{OR}$
Let $x=100$. Then the minuend (the first quantity in the subtraction operation) is

$(x+1)\left(x^{2}-x+1\right)=x^{3}+1,$
and the subtrahend (the quantity being subtracted from the minuend) is

$(x-1)\left(x^{2}+x+1\right)=x^{3}-1 .$
The difference is

$\left(x^{3}+1\right)-\left(x^{3}-1\right)=(\text{A})\boxed{2} .$

raw_content.title: A model used to estimate the time it will take to hike to the top of a mountain on a trail is of the form $T=a L+b G$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants, $T$ is the time in minutes, $L$ is the length of the trail in miles, and $G$ is the altitude gain in feet. The model estimates that it will take 69 minutes to hike to the top if a trail is 1.5 miles long and ascends 800 feet, as well as if a trail is 1.2 miles long and ascends 1100 feet. How many minutes does the model estimate it will take to hike to the top if the trail is 4.2 miles long and ascends 4000 feet?

solution_info.solution_info:
The given data from the first two hikes yield the system of equations

$\begin{aligned} 1.5 a+800 b & =69 \\ 1.2 a+1100 b & =69 . \end{aligned}$
To solve this system, first subtract the second equation from the first equation to get $0.3 a-300 b=0$, which implies $a=1000 b$. Then the first equation becomes $1500 b+800 b=69$, from which $b=\frac{69}{2300}=0.03$, and $a=30$. Therefore the model is $T=30 L+0.03 G$. Substituting the values for the third hike gives $T=30 \cdot 4.2+0.03 \cdot 4000=(\text{B})\boxed{246}$ minutes.

Note: Expressed in words, this commonly used model is "two miles per hour plus a half-hour for each 1000 feet of altitude gain."

raw_content.title: The number 2024 is written as the sum of not necessarily distinct two-digit numbers. What is the least number of two-digit numbers needed to write this sum?

solution_info.solution_info: In order to minimize the number of terms in the sum, the greatest two-digit number, 99 , should be used as many times as possible. Because $20 \cdot 99=1980$, the minimum number of terms is greater than 20 . On the other hand, $2024=20 \cdot 99+44$, so the least number of two-digit numbers needed is $(\text{B})\boxed{21}$.

raw_content.title: A data set containing 20 numbers, some of which are 6 , has mean 45 . When all the 6 s are removed, the data set has mean 66 . How many 6 s were in the original data set?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let the number of 6 s in the original data set be $k$. Numbers in the original data set have sum $20 \cdot 45=900$, and the data set with the 6 s removed has sum $900-6 k$. Thus

$\frac{900-6 k}{20-k}=66$
Solving this equation for $k$ yields $k=(\text{D})\boxed{7}$. For example, the data set could consist of 7 copies of 6 and 13 copies of 66.

raw_content.title: The product of three integers is 60 . What is the least possible positive sum of the three integers?

solution_info.solution_info:
Note that $60=10 \cdot(-1) \cdot(-6)$, and the sum of these factors is 3. It remains to show that no positive sum can be less than 3 . Such a sum would have to consist of one positive integer and two negative integers with smaller absolute value. If the positive integer is greater than or equal to 10 , then the sum is greater than or equal to 3 . The possible sets of factors in this case are $\{10,-6,-1\},\{10,-3,-2\},\{12,-5,-1\},\{15,-4,-1\},\{15,-2,-2\},\{20,-3,-1\},\{30,-2,-1\}$, and $\{60,-1,-1\}$. None of these sets of factors has a sum less than $(\text{B})\boxed{3}$.

The only other possible choices for the positive integer are 5 and 6 , and in neither case is a positive sum possible. Indeed, if the positive integer is 5 , then the only possible set of factors is $\{5,-3,-4\}$. If the positive integer is 6 , then the only possible set of factors is $\{6,-5,-2\}$. In both of these cases, the sum is not positive.

raw_content.title: How many angles $\theta$ with $0 \leq \theta \leq 2 \pi$ satisfy $\log (\sin (3 \theta))+\log (\cos (2 \theta))=0?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Suppose $\theta$ satisfies the equation. Then $\log (\sin (3 \theta) \cdot \cos (2 \theta))=0$. This implies $\sin (3 \theta) \cdot \cos (2 \theta)=1$, so applying the Product-to-Sum Formula

$\sin a \cdot \cos b=\frac{1}{2}(\sin (a+b)+\sin (a-b))$
gives $\frac{1}{2}(\sin (5 \theta)+\sin \theta)=1$. Then $\sin (5 \theta)+\sin \theta=2$, so $\sin (5 \theta)=\sin \theta=1$, and the only possible solution is $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$.

However, this solution is not valid because $\sin (3 \theta)$ is equal to $-1$, and $\log (\sin (3 \theta))$ is not defined.

$\textbf{OR}$
As in the first solution, $\sin (3 \theta) \cdot \cos (2 \theta)=1$. Then either $\sin (3 \theta)=1$ and $\cos (2 \theta)=1$, or $\sin (3 \theta)=-1$ and $\cos (2 \theta)=-1$. However, only the first case is possible because otherwise the logarithms in the equation are not defined. In the first case, $3\theta \in \{\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{5 \pi}{2}, \frac{9 \pi}{2}\}$ and $2 \theta \in\{0,2 \pi, 4 \pi\}$, yielding $\theta \in \{\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{5\pi}{6}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\}$ and $\theta \in\{0, \pi, 2 \pi\}$. The two sets have no common values for $\theta$, so the first case yields no solutions.

raw_content.title: Let $\alpha$ be the radian measure of the smallest angle in a $3-4-5$ right triangle. Let $\beta$ be the radian measure of the smallest angle in a 7-24-25 right triangle. In terms of $\alpha$, what is $\beta$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
Because $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the smallest angles in these triangles, $\sin \alpha=\frac{3}{5}, \cos \alpha=\frac{4}{5}$, $\sin \beta=\frac{7}{25}$, and $\cos \beta=\frac{24}{25}$. By a Double Angle Formula,

$\sin (2 \alpha)=2 \sin \alpha \cdot \cos \alpha=2 \cdot \frac{3}{5} \cdot \frac{4}{5}=\frac{24}{25}=\cos \beta=\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\beta\right)$
Because both $2 \alpha$ and $\beta$ are acute, $2 \alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}-\beta$, so $\beta=(\text{C})\boxed{\frac{\pi}{2}-2 \alpha}$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/73977020e22673b28b2f9a3342f0a39b0a00e35ab806d51cba9ef39f6e1eafbd.jpg]

$\textbf{OR}$
Using complex numbers in polar form, $4+3 i=5(\cos \alpha+i \sin \alpha)$. Squaring gives $7+24 i=$ $25(\cos \alpha+i \sin \alpha)^{2}$. Similarly, $24+7 i=25(\cos \beta+i \sin \beta)$. Multiplying these two equations yields

$\begin{aligned} (7+24 i)(24+7 i) & =25(\cos \alpha+i \sin \alpha)^{2} \cdot 25(\cos \beta+i \sin \beta) \\ 625 i & =625(\cos (2 \alpha+\beta)+i \sin (2 \alpha+\beta)) \\ \cos \frac{\pi}{2}+i \sin \frac{\pi}{2} & =\cos (2 \alpha+\beta)+i \sin (2 \alpha+\beta) . \end{aligned}$
Because both $2 \alpha$ and $\beta$ are acute, $2 \alpha+\beta=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\beta=(\text{C})\boxed{\frac{\pi}{2}-2 \alpha}$.

Note: The angles are $\alpha \approx 36.87^{\circ}$ and $\beta \approx 16.26^{\circ}$.

raw_content.title: The first three terms of a geometric sequence are the integers $a, 720$, and $b$, where $a<720<b$. What is the sum of the digits of the least possible value of $b$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
The prime factorization of 720 is $2^{4} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5$. Let $r=\frac{m}{n}$ be the common ratio of the geometric sequence, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. If $n$ had any prime factor greater than 5 , then $b=720 r$ would not be an integer. Analogously, if $m$ had any prime factor greater than 5 , then $a=\frac{720}{r}$ would not be an integer. It follows that $r=2^{i} \cdot 3^{j} \cdot 5^{k}$, where $i, j$, and $k$ are (not necessarily positive) integers. Furthermore, $|i| \leq 4,|j| \leq 2$, and $|k| \leq 1$.

To minimize the value of $b$, it suffices to minimize the value of $r>1$. Taking $r=\frac{16}{15}=2^{4} \cdot 3^{-1} \cdot 5^{-1}$ yields the sequence $675,720,768$. To check that no lesser values of $r$ exist, first observe that $\frac{17}{16}$ is not a possible value for $r$, so both $n$ and $m$ are greater than 17 . This means that $m$ and $n$ must borrow at least two prime factors each from 720 , but 720 has only three distinct prime factors, so this is impossible. It follows that the least possible value of $b$ is 768 , and the requested sum of digits is $7+6+8=(\text{E})\boxed{21}$.

raw_content.title: The graph of $y=e^{x+1}+e^{-x}-2$ has an axis of symmetry. What is the reflection of the point $\left(-1, \frac{1}{2}\right)$ over this axis?

solution_info.solution_info: Let $f(x)=e^{x+1}+e^{-x}-2$. Because $f(x)$ approaches infinity as $|x|$ increases without bound, the only possible axis of symmetry is a vertical line. If the axis of symmetry has equation $x=$ $c$, then $f(x)=f(2 c-x)$ for every real $x$, which is equivalent to $e \cdot e^{x}+e^{-x}=e^{2 c+1} e^{-x}+e^{-2 c} e^{x}$. Multiplying through by $e^{x}$ and simplifying gives $\left(e-e^{-2 c}\right) e^{2 x}=e^{2 c+1}-1$. Because this equation holds for all $x$, it follows that $e-e^{-2 c}=0$ and $e^{2 c+1}-1=0$. Thus $c=-\frac{1}{2}$. The reflection of $\left(-1, \frac{1}{2}\right)$ with respect to the vertical line $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ is $(\text{D})\boxed{\left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right)}$.

raw_content.title:
The numbers, in order, of each row and the numbers, in order, of each column of a $5 \times 5$ array of integers form an arithmetic progression of length 5 . The numbers in positions $(5,5),(2,4),(4,3)$, and $(3,1)$ are $0,48,16$, and 12 , respectively. What number is in position $(1,2) ?$

$\left[\begin{array}{ccccc} \cdot & ? & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 48 & \cdot \\ 12 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\ \cdot & \cdot & 16 & \cdot & \cdot \\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 0 \end{array}\right]$

solution_info.solution_info:

$a_{41}=\frac{a_{31}+a_{51}}{2}=\frac{12+4 d}{2}=6+2 d$
The arithmetic progression in column 4 gives

$a_{44}=\frac{2 a_{54}+a_{24}}{3}=\frac{2 d+48}{3}=\frac{2}{3} d+16$
Row 4 gives

$a_{43}=16=\frac{2 a_{44}+a_{41}}{3}=\frac{\frac{4}{3} d+32+6+2 d}{3}$
which implies $48=\frac{10}{3} d+38$, so $d=3$. Filling in column 3 with common difference $16-6=10$ and column 1 with difference $12-12=0$ produces $a_{13}=46$ and $a_{11}=12$. Finally,

$a_{12}=\frac{a_{13}+a_{11}}{2}=\frac{46+12}{2}=(\text{C})\boxed{29}$
The full array looks like this:

$\left[\begin{array}{ccccc} 12 & \underline{\mathbf{2 9}} & 46 & 63 & 80 \\ 12 & 24 & 36 & \mathbf{4 8} & 60 \\ \mathbf{1 2} & 19 & 26 & 33 & 40 \\ 12 & 14 & \mathbf{1 6} & 18 & 20 \\ 12 & 9 & 6 & 3 & \mathbf{0} \end{array}\right]$

raw_content.title:
The roots of $x^{3}+2 x^{2}-x+3$ are $p, q$, and $r$. What is the value of

$\left(p^{2}+4\right)\left(q^{2}+4\right)\left(r^{2}+4\right) ?$

solution_info.solution_info:
By Vieta's Formulas,

$\begin{aligned} p+q+r & =-2 \\ p q+p r+q r & =-1, \text { and } \\ p q r & =-3 \end{aligned}$
The expression to be evaluated is

$\left(p^{2}+4\right)\left(q^{2}+4\right)\left(r^{2}+4\right)=p^{2} q^{2} r^{2}+4\left(p^{2} q^{2}+p^{2} r^{2}+q^{2} r^{2}\right)+16\left(p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}\right)+64$
The first term is

$p^{2} q^{2} r^{2}=(p q r)^{2}=(-3)^{2}=9$
To find the second term, note that

$(p q+p r+q r)^{2}=p^{2} q^{2}+p^{2} r^{2}+q^{2} r^{2}+2 \operatorname{pqr}(p+q+r)$
Rearranging and substituting yields

$p^{2} q^{2}+p^{2} r^{2}+q^{2} r^{2}=(-1)^{2}-2(-3)(-2)=-11$
For the third term,

$(p+q+r)^{2}=p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}+2(p q+p r+q r)$
so

$p^{2}+q^{2}+r^{2}=(-2)^{2}-2(-1)=6$
Therefore

$\left(p^{2}+4\right)\left(q^{2}+4\right)\left(r^{2}+4\right)=9+4 \cdot(-11)+16 \cdot 6+64=125$
With $i=\sqrt{-1}$, the given expression can be factored as

$\begin{aligned} \left(p^{2}+4\right)\left(q^{2}+4\right)\left(r^{2}+4\right) & =(p-2 i)(p+2 i)(q-2 i)(q+2 i)(r-2 i)(r+2 i) \\ & =[(p-2 i)(q-2 i)(r-2 i)] \cdot[(p+2 i)(q+2 i)(r+2 i)] \end{aligned}$
Let $f(x)$ be the given polynomial. Then $f(x)=-(p-x)(q-x)(r-x)$ and

$-f(2 i)=(p-2 i)(q-2 i)(r-2 i)$
which is the first bracketed expression above. Furthermore

$f(-x)=(-x-p)(-x-q)(-x-r)=-(p+x)(q+x)(r+x)$
Therefore

$-f(-x)=(p+x)(q+x)(r+x)$
It follows that

$-f(-2 i)=(p+2 i)(q+2 i)(r+2 i)$
the second bracketed expression above. Hence

$\left(p^{2}+4\right)\left(q^{2}+4\right)\left(r^{2}+4\right)=-f(2 i) \cdot(-f(-2 i))=f(2 i) \cdot f(-2 i) .$
Because

$f(2 i)=(2 i)^{3}+2(2 i)^{2}-(2 i)+3=-8 i-8-2 i+3=-10 i-5$
and

$f(-2 i)=(-2 i)^{3}+2(-2 i)^{2}-(-2 i)+3=8 i-8+2 i+3=10 i-5,$
the requested product is

$f(2 i) \cdot f(-2 i)=(-10 i-5)(10 i-5)=(\text{D})\boxed{125} .$
Note: The roots of the polynomial are approximately $-2.757,0.379+0.972 i$, and $0.379-0.972 i$.

raw_content.title: A set of 12 tokens- 3 red, 2 white, 1 blue, and 6 black-is to be distributed at random to 3 game players, 4 tokens per player. The probability that some player gets all the red tokens, another player gets all the white tokens, and the remaining player gets the blue token can be written as $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. What is $m+n$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
The situation can be modeled by arranging the 12 tokens in a row, with the first player receiving the first 4 tokens, the second player receiving the next 4 tokens, and the third player receiving the last 4 tokens. There are $\frac{12!}{3!\cdot 2!\cdot 1!\cdot 6!}$ such arrangements. The given conditions are satisfied if and only if the red tokens appear among the first 4 positions, the white tokens appear among the next 4 positions, and the blue token appears among the last 4 positions, or some permutation of the groups of 4. There are $\binom{4}{3} \cdot\binom{4}{2} \cdot\binom{4}{1} \cdot 3$ ! ways for this to happen. The required probability is therefore

$\frac{4 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 3!\cdot 2!\cdot 1!\cdot 6!}{12!}=\frac{4}{385}$
and the requested sum is $4+385=(\text{C})\boxed{389}$.

raw_content.title: Integers $a, b$, and $c$ satisfy $a b+c=100, b c+a=87$, and $c a+b=60$. What is $a b+b c+c a$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
Notice that the difference between $100$ and $87$ is $13$, a prime number. This fact will help to simplify the problem. Subtract the second equation from the first to get

$\begin{aligned} 13 & =(a b+c)-(b c+a) \\ & =a b-b c-a+c \\ & =b(a-c)-(a-c) \\ & =(b-1)(a-c) \end{aligned}$
Thus $b-1= \pm 1$ or $b-1= \pm 13$.

If $b-1=-1$, then $b=0$, implying $c=100, a=87$, and $c a=60$, which is impossible.

If $b-1=1$, then $b=2$ and $a-c=13$, implying $c a=58=2 \cdot 29$, which cannot be true if $a-c=13$.

If $b-1=13$, then $b=14$ and $a-c=1$, implying $c a=46=2 \cdot 23$, which cannot be true if $a-c=1$.

If $b-1=-13$, then $b=-12$ and $a-c=-1$, implying $c a=72$, which is satisfied when $a=-9$ and $c=-8$. In fact, $a=-9, b=-12$, and $c=-8$ satisfies all three equations.

The requested value is $a b+b c+c a=(-9)(-12)+(-12)(-8)+(-8)(-9)=108+96+72=(\text{D})\boxed{276}$.

Note: There are also four noninteger solutions. When written in the form $(a, b, c)$, these solutions are approximately $(0.594,0.869,99.484),(1.715,57.455,1.484),(7.477,12.525,6.349)$, and $(86.214, 1.152, 0.683)$.

raw_content.title:
On top of a rectangular card with sides of length 1 and $2+\sqrt{3}$, an identical card is placed so that two of their diagonals line up, as shown ( $\overline{A C}$, in this case).

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/2d21c093c1afe07b3023991fecdd3fc47cd3580871e8475a9fd269d85b60e2b5.jpg]

Continue the process, adding a third card to the second, and so on, lining up successive diagonals after rotating clockwise. In total, how many cards must be used until a vertex of a new card lands exactly on the vertex labeled $B$ in the figure?
raw_content.option_e: No new vertex will land on $B$

solution_info.solution_info:
Note that the common diagonal is a diameter of the circle that will ultimately circumscribe the collection of rectangles. Each rectangle is composed of four chords of the circle, and the set of outermost chords will form a regular $n$-gon if a vertex lands on $B$. Because each new card contributes two sides of the polygon, the problem is asking for $\frac{n}{2}$. Let $O$ be the center of the circle.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/4a766bc541762a863aed3498ee7d04a73033f64c15c0088c0e74b0504348e78f.jpg]

Let $\theta=\angle A C B$. Then the measure of minor arc \wideparen{A B} is $2 \theta$, and $n=\frac{360^{\circ}}{2 \theta}$. Because $A B=1$ and $B C=2+\sqrt{3}$,

$\tan \theta=\frac{1}{2+\sqrt{3}}=2-\sqrt{3} .$
Each card is rotated through an angle $\angle A O B=2 \theta$ compared to the previous card. A Double Angle Formula gives

$\tan 2 \theta=\frac{2 \tan \theta}{1-\tan ^{2} \theta}=\frac{2(2-\sqrt{3})}{1-(2-\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} .$
This value is recognizable as $\tan 30^{\circ}$, so $2 \theta=30^{\circ}$ and $n=\frac{360}{30}=12$. The polygon is a dodecagon. It will take just $\frac{n}{2}=(\text{A})\boxed{6}$ cards to complete the dodecagon and have a new vertex land on vertex $B$, as illustrated below.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/0d958826b0c5fd476b6aeff2a5479e284eee862ef8a2c244d0eef6f54e8d8ebd.jpg]

raw_content.title: Cyclic quadrilateral $A B C D$ has lengths $B C=C D=3$ and $D A=5$ with $\angle C D A=120^{\circ}$. What is the length of the shorter diagonal of $A B C D$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
Place the figure in the coordinate plane with $D=(0,0)$ and $A=(5,0)$. Because $\angle C D A=120^{\circ}$ and $C D=3$, it follows that $C=\left(-\frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{3}\right)$. The perpendicular bisectors of $\overline{C D}$ and $\overline{A D}$ intersect at the center of the circumscribing circle. The midpoint of $\overline{C D}$ is $\left(-\frac{3}{4}, \frac{3}{4} \sqrt{3}\right)$. The line through $\overline{C D}$ has slope $-\sqrt{3}$, so a line perpendicular to that has slope $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$. The perpendicular bisector of $\overline{C D}$ therefore has equation

$y-\frac{3}{4} \sqrt{3}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\left(x+\frac{3}{4}\right)$
The perpendicular bisector of $\overline{A D}$ has equation $x=\frac{5}{2}$. Solving this system of equations locates the center of the circumscribing circle at $O\left(\frac{5}{2}, \frac{11}{6} \sqrt{3}\right)$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/7696ee7fa92277f8e092582f3bebee1063d5baef11a971fb28c737c0c35c2231.jpg]

By the Distance Formula, the radius of the circle is

$r=O D=\sqrt{\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{11}{6} \sqrt{3}\right)^{2}}=\frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{3} .$
Let $\theta$ be the measure of $\angle B C O$. By the Law of Cosines applied to $\triangle B C O$,

$\frac{49}{3}=B O^{2}=B C^{2}+C O^{2}-2 B C \cdot C O \cos \theta=9+\frac{49}{3}-2 \cdot 3 \cdot \frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{3} \cos \theta$
which gives $\cos \theta=\frac{3}{14} \sqrt{3}$. A Double Angle Formula then gives $\cos 2 \theta=2 \cdot \frac{27}{196}-1=-\frac{71}{98}$. Triangles $\triangle B O C$ and $\triangle C O D$ are congruent isosceles triangles, so $\angle B C D$ has measure $2 \theta$. By the Law of Cosines applied to $\triangle B C D$,

$B D^{2}=B C^{2}+C D^{2}-2 B C \cdot C D \cos 2 \theta=9+9-2 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot\left(-\frac{71}{98}\right)=\frac{1521}{49}=\left(\frac{3 \cdot 13}{7}\right)^{2},$
so $B D=\frac{39}{7}$. The Law of Cosines applied to $\triangle A D C$ gives $A C=7$, so the shorter diagonal has length $(\text{D})\boxed{\frac{39}{7}}$.

$\textbf{OR}$
The Law of Cosines applied to $\triangle A D C$ gives

$C A^{2}=3^{2}+5^{2}-2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot \cos 120^{\circ} .$
Because $\cos 120^{\circ}=-\frac{1}{2}$, diagonal $\overline{A C}$ has length $\sqrt{9+25+15}=7$. Because $A B C D$ is cyclic, $\angle A B C$ is supplementary to $\angle A D C$, so $\angle A B C=60^{\circ}$. The Law of Cosines applied to $\triangle A B C$ gives

$7^{2}=3^{2}+B A^{2}-2 \cdot 3 \cdot B A \cdot \cos 60^{\circ}$
Simplifying yields $B A^{2}-3 \cdot B A-40=0$, so $B A=8$. By Ptolemy's Theorem

$C A \cdot B D=B A \cdot C D+B C \cdot A D$
Substituting gives $7 \cdot B D=8 \cdot 3+3 \cdot 5$, so $B D=(\text{D})\boxed{\frac{39}{7}}$, which is less than the length of diagonal $\overline{A C}$.

raw_content.title: Points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen uniformly and independently at random on sides $\overline{A B}$ and $\overline{A C}$, respectively, of equilateral triangle $\triangle A B C$. Which of the following intervals contains the probability that the area of $\triangle A P Q$ is less than half the area of $\triangle A B C?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Without loss of generality let $A B=A C=B C=1$; then the area of $\triangle A B C$ is $\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{3}$. Let $x=A P$ and $y=A Q$. Then the area of $\triangle A P Q$ is

$\frac{1}{2} x y \cdot \sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{3} \cdot x y$
The probability that the area of $\triangle A P Q$ is less than half the area of $\triangle A B C$ is therefore the probability that $x y<\frac{1}{2}$. Graph the curve $x y=\frac{1}{2}$ in the unit square whose lower left corner is at the origin, as shown. Note that the curve passes through the points $\left(\frac{1}{2}, 1\right)$ and $\left(1, \frac{1}{2}\right)$ and is concave up on the interval $\frac{1}{2}<x<1$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/93edd2ea2106ddf6c9b891fc5fa6997f8008b021eff57ac9a4be114587cf1190.jpg]

The probability that $x y>\frac{1}{2}$ is the area of the upper right "fat triangular" region with curved longest side, which is less than $\frac{1}{4}$ but greater than $\frac{1}{8}$. Therefore the probability that $x y<\frac{1}{2}$ lies between $1-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{4}$ and $1-\frac{1}{8}=\frac{7}{8}$.

Note: The required area can be calculated to be $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \ln 2 \approx 0.85$.

raw_content.title:
Suppose that $a_{1}=2$ and the sequence $\left(a_{n}\right)$ satisfies the recurrence relation

$\frac{a_{n}-1}{n-1}=\frac{a_{n-1}+1}{(n-1)+1}$
for all $n \geq 2$. What is the greatest integer less than or equal to

$\sum_{n=1}^{100} a_{n}^{2} ?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Computing the first few terms of this sequence gives $a_{1}=2, a_{2}=\frac{5}{2}, a_{3}=\frac{10}{3}$, and $a_{4}=\frac{17}{4}$, so it appears that $a_{n}=n+\frac{1}{n}$. Indeed, this is correct, because the recurrence relation is satisfied:

$\frac{a_{n-1}+1}{(n-1)+1}=\frac{n-1+\frac{1}{n-1}+1}{n}=1+\frac{1}{n(n-1)}=\frac{n-1}{n-1}+\frac{\frac{1}{n}}{n-1}=\frac{a_{n}-1}{n-1} .$
Then

$\begin{aligned} \sum_{n=1}^{100} a_{n}^{2} & =\sum_{n=1}^{100}\left(n^{2}+2+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right) \\ & =\frac{100 \cdot 101 \cdot 201}{6}+200+r \\ & =\frac{2030100+1200}{6}+r \\ & =338,550+r, \end{aligned}$
where $r=\sum_{n=1}^{100} \frac{1}{n^{2}}$. But by a telescoping sum argument,

$1<r<1+\sum_{n=2}^{100} \frac{1}{n(n-1)}=2-\frac{1}{100}<2$
Thus $\sum_{n=1}^{100} a_{n}^{2}$ is between 338,551 and 338,552 , and the requested greatest integer is $(\text{B})\boxed{338,551}$.

Note: One could also estimate $\sum_{n=1}^{100} \frac{1}{n^{2}}$ by using the fact that

$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^{2}}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{6} \approx 1.645$
as proved by Euler in the 18th century.

Carl places 1 -inch toothpicks along some of the sides of the squares to create a closed loop that does not intersect itself. The numbers in the cells indicate the number of sides of that square that are to be covered by toothpicks, and any number of toothpicks are allowed if no number is written. In how many ways can Carl place the toothpicks?

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/3ef5c5bf36b186ab985aee2cf59e29199d5ea2b6d502053ae589fdd3ae8a5ba0.jpg]

solution_info.solution_info:

Otherwise, wherever the loop crosses the middle row, it must proceed straight in both directions after the middle row. This divides the dotted grid into two connected components, and both ends of the loop must enter the same connected component. It follows that the loop must cross one of the leftmost two columns and one of the rightmost two columns for a total of four configurations.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/475385c23cf1003634b71fc46e5d20c2e2645613b17aabd084958a870151053b.jpg]

For each 1 , the loop can cover either the top edge or the bottom edge. These choices are independent of each other, so the number of ways to connect both ends of the loop is $2^{n}$. The figure below demonstrates one possibility when $n=6$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/34093bb5e9134c53464a99e2664ab2b9e4a980f20a20ec9c8d28258ea25ff544.jpg]

Of the four possibilities for what happens at the ends, one gives $n=6$, two give $n=5$, and one gives $n=4$. The total number of solutions is

raw_content.title:
What is the value of

$\tan ^{2} \frac{\pi}{16} \cdot \tan ^{2} \frac{3 \pi}{16}+\tan ^{2} \frac{\pi}{16} \cdot \tan ^{2} \frac{5 \pi}{16}+\tan ^{2} \frac{3 \pi}{16} \cdot \tan ^{2} \frac{7 \pi}{16}+\tan ^{2} \frac{5 \pi}{16} \cdot \tan ^{2} \frac{7 \pi}{16} ?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $\theta=\frac{\pi}{16}$, and let $c=\cos \theta, s=\sin \theta$, and $t=\tan \theta$. Then

$e^{8 i \theta}=e^{\frac{\pi}{2} \cdot i}=(c+i s)^{8}=0+1 i$
Expanding the binomial and taking the real part gives

$0=1 c^{8}-28 c^{6} s^{2}+70 c^{4} s^{4}-28 c^{2} s^{6}+1 s^{8}$
Divide by $c^{8}$ to get

$1-28 t^{2}+70 t^{4}-28 t^{6}+1 t^{8}=0$
and let $p(t)=1-28 t^{2}+70 t^{4}-28 t^{6}+1 t^{8}$. In other words, $t=\tan \theta$ and $-t=-\tan \theta$ are roots of the polynomial

$p(x)=1-28 x^{2}+70 x^{4}-28 x^{6}+1 x^{8}$
The same argument with $\theta=\frac{\pi}{16}$ replaced by $\theta_{k}=\frac{k \pi}{16}$ shows that $t_{k}=\tan \theta_{k}$ is also a root of $p(x)$ for $k \in\{1,3,5,7\}$. This holds because $\left(c_{k}+i s_{k}\right)^{8}=0 \pm 1 i$ when $c_{k}=\cos (k \theta)$ and $s_{k}=\sin (k \theta)$. In each case $8 k \equiv 8(\bmod 16)$. Therefore $x=\tan (k \theta)$ is a root of $p(x)$ whenever

$x^{2} \in\left\{\tan ^{2} \theta, \tan ^{2}(3 \theta), \tan ^{2}(5 \theta), \tan ^{2}(7 \theta)\right\}$
This accounts for all 8 roots, so it must be that

$p(x)=\left(x^{2}-\tan ^{2} \theta\right)\left(x^{2}-\tan ^{2}(3 \theta)\right)\left(x^{2}-\tan ^{2}(5 \theta)\right)\left(x^{2}-\tan ^{2}(7 \theta)\right)$
Examining the $x^{4}$ term in the two expressions for $p(x)$ reveals that

$\begin{aligned} \tan ^{2} \theta \cdot \tan ^{2}(3 \theta)+\tan ^{2} \theta \cdot \tan ^{2}(5 \theta) & +\tan ^{2} \theta \cdot \tan ^{2}(7 \theta)+\tan ^{2}(3 \theta) \cdot \tan ^{2}(5 \theta) \\ & +\tan ^{2}(3 \theta) \cdot \tan ^{2}(7 \theta)+\tan ^{2}(5 \theta) \cdot \tan ^{2}(7 \theta)=70 \end{aligned}$
The identity $\tan \theta \cdot \tan \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\tan \theta \cdot \cot \theta=1$ implies that

$\tan ^{2} \theta \cdot \tan ^{2}(7 \theta)=\tan ^{2}(3 \theta) \cdot \tan ^{2}(5 \theta)=1$
Subtracting those two terms from the previous expression gives

$\tan ^{2} \theta \cdot \tan ^{2}(3 \theta)+\tan ^{2} \theta \cdot \tan ^{2}(5 \theta)+\tan ^{2}(3 \theta) \cdot \tan ^{2}(7 \theta)+\tan ^{2}(5 \theta) \cdot \tan ^{2}(7 \theta)=(\text{B})\boxed{68}$

raw_content.title: A disphenoid is a tetrahedron whose triangular faces are congruent to one another. What is the least total surface area of a disphenoid whose faces are scalene triangles with integer side lengths?

solution_info.solution_info:
First note that adjacent faces must be rotations of one another to create a disphenoid (see the figure below). If they were instead mirrored, then the other two faces would be isosceles (and be neither scalene nor congruent to the others, as required).

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/cb479f5fa6742c24ef4001da8996742be1e5d60269323a82673d3924e2ff9ca2.jpg]

Next, to determine what triangles could form a disphenoid, let the positive integer side lengths be $a$, $b$, and $c$, with $a<b<c$. Consider two faces of the tetrahedron that have their sides of length $c$ in common. That common edge can be thought of as a "hinge" between two faces. If those two faces were laid flat, they would form a parallelogram with one diagonal of length $c$. When folded over the hinge, the other diagonal of the parallelogram becomes two sides of a triangle whose third side is the last edge of the tetrahedron. (Note that this last edge must have length $c$ to create the disphenoid.) If the sides of length $a$ and $b$ formed a right angle, then the parallelogram would be a rectangle, and the other diagonal would also have length $c$. A tetrahedron formed by folding the triangles over the hinge would have its last edge shorter than $c$, making it not a disphenoid. If instead the sides of length $a$ and $b$ formed an obtuse angle, the other diagonal would be shorter than $c$, and folding would make the last edge shorter yet (and again not a disphenoid). Thus the faces must be acute to form a disphenoid.

To minimize the surface area, $a, b$, and $c$ must be the least distinct integers that form an acute triangle. Note that 2, 3, and 4 form an obtuse triangle (because $2^{2}+3^{2}<4^{2}$ ); and 3, 4, and 5 form a right triangle. However, $4^{2}+5^{2}=41>36=6^{2}$, so 4,5 , and 6 form an acute triangle with the least area. The area of one face can be computed using Heron's Formula. The triangle's semiperimeter is $\frac{4+5+6}{2}=\frac{15}{2}$, and the disphenoid's total surface area is

$\begin{aligned} 4 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{15}{2}\left(\frac{15}{2}-4\right)\left(\frac{15}{2}-5\right)\left(\frac{15}{2}-6\right)} & =4 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1}{16} \cdot 15(15-8)(15-10)(15-12)} \\ & =\frac{4}{4} \cdot \sqrt{15 \cdot 7 \cdot 5 \cdot 3}=15 \sqrt{7} \end{aligned}$
Another way to find the area of a face is to use the formula $\frac{1}{2} a b \sin \gamma$. By the Law of Cosines,

$\cos \gamma=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}}{2 a b}=\frac{4^{2}+5^{2}-6^{2}}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 5}=\frac{1}{8} .$
Then

$\sin \gamma=\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{64}}=\frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{8}$
Therefore the area of one face is

$\frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdot \frac{3 \sqrt{7}}{8}=\frac{15 \sqrt{7}}{4}$
and the total surface area is $(\text{D})\boxed{15\sqrt{7}}$.

raw_content.title:
A graph is symmetric about a line if the graph remains unchanged after reflection in that line. For how many quadruples of integers $(a, b, c, d)$, where $|a|,|b|,|c|,|d| \leq 5$ and $c$ and $d$ are not both 0 , is the graph of

$y=\frac{a x+b}{c x+d}$
symmetric about the line $y=x$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
There are two cases, depending on whether the denominator of the fraction is constant.

CASE 1. Suppose that $c=0$. Then the graph of $y=\frac{a x+b}{d}$ is a line. It is symmetric with respect to the line $y=x$ if the slope of the line is 1 and the line passes through the origin, or the slope is -1 . A line with slope 1 that passes through the origin occurs if $a=d \neq 0$ and $b=0$. There are 10 possible values of $a$. The slope is -1 if $d=-a \neq 0$. There are 10 possible values of $a$, and 11 possible values of $b$, which gives 110 possibilities. This gives a total of 120 possibilities in Case 1 .

CASE 2. Suppose that $c \neq 0$. The quantity $y=\frac{a x+b}{c x+d}$ tends to $\frac{a}{c}$ as $x \rightarrow \pm \infty$. This is a horizontal asymptote. The degree of the polynomial in the numerator can be reduced by subtracting this asymptotic value:

$y-\frac{a}{c}=\frac{a x+b}{c x+d}-\frac{a}{c}=\frac{a c x+b c-a(c x+d)}{c(c x+d)}=\frac{b c-a d}{c(c x+d)}=\frac{\Delta}{x-\frac{-d}{c}}$
where

$\Delta=\frac{b c-a d}{c^{2}}$
If $\Delta=0$, then the graph of $y$ consists of the points $\left(x, \frac{a}{c}\right)$, except that the point $\left(\frac{-d}{c}, \frac{a}{c}\right)$ is missing because the formula reads $\frac{0}{0}$ when $x=-\frac{d}{c}$. In any case, this set of points is not symmetric with respect to the line $y=x$. From now on, assume that $\Delta \neq 0$. Multiply both sides by $x-\frac{-d}{c}$ to find that

$\left(x-\frac{-d}{c}\right)\left(y-\frac{a}{c}\right)=\Delta$
Note that $x-\frac{-d}{c} \neq 0$ because $\Delta \neq 0$. Thus, if it were desired, both sides of the new equation could be divided by $x-\frac{-c}{d}$ to recover the former equation. Hence the set of pairs $(x, y)$ that satisfy the former equation is exactly the same as the set of $(x, y)$ that satisfy the new equation, which determines a rectangular hyperbola. This hyperbola is symmetric with respect to the line $y=x$ if and only if its center $\left(\frac{a}{c},-\frac{d}{c}\right)$ lies on this line of symmetry. That is, $d=-a$. Thus $\Delta \neq 0$ if and only if $b c+a^{2} \neq 0$.

If $a=0$, then $b$ and $c$ are free to take on any nonzero values, which gives $10 \cdot 10=100$ quadruples $(0, b, c, 0)$. If $a \neq 0$, then because $d=-a$ and $c \neq 0$, there are $10 \cdot 11 \cdot 10=1100$ quadruples $(a, b, c,-a)$ to consider. Note that $b c+a^{2}=0$ if and only if either $|a|=|b|=|c|$ and $b$ and $c$ have opposite signs, which is $10 \cdot 2=20$ cases, or $|a|=2$ and $(b, c)=( \pm 4, \mp 1)$ or $( \pm 1, \mp 4)$, which is $2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2=8$ additional cases. Thus the total number of possibilities in Case 2 is $100+1100-(20+8)=$ 1172.

In all there are $120+1172=(\text{B})\boxed{1292}$ quadruples satisfying the given conditions.

Note: Functions of the form $y=\frac{a x+b}{c x+d}$ with $a d-b c \neq 0$ are known as "linear-fractional" or "Möbius". They arise in complex analysis and in number theory.
