solution_info.solution_info: After $n$ steps, a total of $1+2+3+\cdots+n=\frac{1}{2} n(n+1)$ balls have been deposited. In particular, after step $n=63$, a total of $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 63 \cdot 64=2016$ balls have been deposited. The next batch of 64 balls will include ball 2024. Because 64 has remainder 4 when divided by 5, ball 2024 is deposited in bin $(\text{D})\boxed{D}$.

raw_content.title: The national debt of the United States is on track to reach $5 \times 10^{13}$ dollars by 2033. How many digits does this number of dollars have when written as a numeral in base 5 ? (The approximation of $\log _{10} 5$ as 0.7 is sufficient for this problem.)

solution_info.solution_info:
The number of digits required to write the positive integer $n$ in base $b$ is $1+\log _{b} n$, rounded down to an integer. Therefore the required value is the floor of

$1+\log _{5}\left(5 \cdot 10^{13}\right)=1+\log _{5} 5+13 \log _{5} 10=1+1+13 \cdot \frac{1}{\log _{10} 5} \approx 2+\frac{13}{0.7}=20.5 \ldots$
which is $(\text{B})\boxed{20}$.

$\textbf{OR}$
It is possible to convert a positive integer to base 5 by repeatedly dividing by 5 and recording the remainders. This list of remainders in reverse order is the required numeral. Here $5 \cdot 10^{13}=2^{13} \cdot 5^{14}$. Performing this calculation gives a remainder of 0 for the first 14 iterations. The following table gives the remaining 6 iterations:

$\begin{array}{|r|r|r|} \hline dividend & quotient & remainder \\ \hline 8192 & 1638 & 2 \\ \hline 1638 & 327 & 3 \\ \hline 327 & 65 & 2 \\ \hline 65 & 13 & 0 \\ \hline 13 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline 2 & 0 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array}$
Therefore $50,000,000,000,000_{\text {ten }}=23,023,200,000,000,000,000_{\text {five }}$, a numeral with $(\text{B})\boxed{20}$ digits.

Expanding and simplifying yields $a^{2}-8 a-4 b+16=0$. Because the areas of triangles $\triangle W X M$ and $\triangle W A Z$ are equal, $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 a=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 8 b$, so $a=2 b$. raw_content.title: Let $x_{n}=\sin ^{2}\left(n^{\circ}\right)$. What is the mean of $x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{90}$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
The required mean is

$\frac{1}{90} \sum_{n=1}^{90} \sin ^{2}\left(n^{\circ}\right)$
Group the summands into 44 pairs plus two additional terms as follows:

$\begin{aligned} \sin ^{2}\left(1^{\circ}\right)+\sin ^{2}\left(89^{\circ}\right) & =\sin ^{2}\left(1^{\circ}\right)+\cos ^{2}\left(1^{\circ}\right)=1 \\ \sin ^{2}\left(2^{\circ}\right)+\sin ^{2}\left(88^{\circ}\right) & =\sin ^{2}\left(2^{\circ}\right)+\cos ^{2}\left(2^{\circ}\right)=1 \\ \sin ^{2}\left(3^{\circ}\right)+\sin ^{2}\left(87^{\circ}\right) & =\sin ^{2}\left(3^{\circ}\right)+\cos ^{2}\left(3^{\circ}\right)=1 \\ \vdots & \\ \sin ^{2}\left(44^{\circ}\right)+\sin ^{2}\left(46^{\circ}\right) & =\sin ^{2}\left(44^{\circ}\right)+\cos ^{2}\left(44^{\circ}\right)=1 \\ \sin ^{2}\left(45^{\circ}\right) & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \sin ^{2}\left(90^{\circ}\right) & =1 \end{aligned}$
This gives a sum of $45 \frac{1}{2}=\frac{91}{2}$, so the mean is $\frac{1}{90} \cdot \frac{91}{2}=(\text{E})\boxed{\frac{91}{180}}$.

raw_content.title: Suppose $z$ is a complex number with positive imaginary part, with real part greater than 1 , and with $|z|=2$. In the complex plane, the four values $0, z, z^{2}$, and $z^{3}$ are the vertices of a quadrilateral with area 15 . What is the imaginary part of $z$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $\theta$ be the argument of $z$. Because $|z|=2$ and the real part of $z$ is greater than 1 , it follows that $\theta$ is less than $60^{\circ}$. This ensures that the imaginary parts of $z^{2}$ and $z^{3}$ are positive and all the vertices of the quadrilateral other than 0 lie in the upper half-plane. Thus the area of the quadrilateral is the sum of the areas of the triangle with vertices $0, z$, and $z^{2}$ and the triangle with vertices $0, z^{2}$, and $z^{3}$. See the figure.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/94bcd4eb670b475caa887ef0f822ddf3c216ed010572f38d84e8fd1fea34dbba.jpg]

Because the area of a triangle with side lengths $a$ and $b$ with included angle $\alpha$ is $\frac{1}{2} a b \sin \alpha$, the area of the quadrilateral must be

$\frac{1}{2}\left(|z| \cdot|z|^{2} \cdot \sin \theta+|z|^{2} \cdot|z|^{3} \cdot \sin \theta\right)=20 \sin \theta=15$
It follows that $\sin \theta=\frac{3}{4}$, and the imaginary part of $z$ is $2 \cdot \sin \theta=(\text{D})\boxed{\frac{3}{2}}$.

raw_content.title:
There are real numbers $x, y, h$, and $k$ that satisfy the system of equations

$\begin{aligned} x^{2}+y^{2}-6 x-8 y & =h \\ x^{2}+y^{2}-10 x+4 y & =k \end{aligned}$
What is the minimum possible value of $h+k$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
Adding the two equations and then completing the squares gives

$2(x-4)^{2}+2(y-1)^{2}=h+k+32+2$
To ensure a real solution, it follows that $h+k$ is at least -34 . This solution can be obtained by setting $x=4$ and $y=1$, in which case $h=4^{2}+1^{2}-6 \cdot 4-8 \cdot 1=-15$ and $k=4^{2}+1^{2}-10 \cdot 4+4 \cdot 1=-19$. The requested minimum is therefore $(\text{C})\boxed{-34}$ .

$\textbf{OR}$
Completing the squares gives

$(x-3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=h+25$
and

$(x-5)^{2}+(y+2)^{2}=k+29$
Thus the graphs of these two equations are circles with centers at $(3,4)$ and $(5,-2)$. The values of $h$ and $k$ are minimized when the two circles are externally tangent and have equal radii, that is, when the radii are half the distance between the two centers of the circles. See the note for further justification.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/49d545f663ffc64a82f79ad7321b827250813d1fab54fa359837ed54867e9b12.jpg]

Thus the radii are both $\frac{1}{2} \cdot \sqrt{(3-5)^{2}+(4+2)^{2}}=\sqrt{10}$. Therefore $h+25=k+29=10$, so $h+k=20-25-29=-34$. The (unique) solution of the system is $(x, y, h, k)=(4,1,-15,-19)$.

Note: The claim in the solution follows from the fact that for two positive real numbers, their quadratic mean is greater than or equal to their arithmetic mean. Indeed, if $\sqrt{h+25}+\sqrt{k+29}=2 \sqrt{10}$, then

$\sqrt{\frac{h+k+54}{2}} \geq \frac{\sqrt{h+25}+\sqrt{k+29}}{2}=\sqrt{10}$
so $h+k \geq(\text{C})\boxed{-34}$.

raw_content.title: How many different remainders can result when the 100 th power of an integer is divided by 125 ?

solution_info.solution_info:
Write $N=5 k+r$ for $r=0,1,2,3$, or 4. If $r=0$, then $N=5 k$ and $N^{100}$ is divisible by 125 , so the remainder is 0 . If $r=1,2,3$, or 4 , then $N^{2}=25 k^{2}+10 r k+r^{2}=5 m \pm 1$ for some integer $m$. Now use the Binomial Theorem:

$\begin{aligned} N^{100}=\left(N^{2}\right)^{50}=(5 m \pm 1)^{50}=(5 m)^{50} & \pm 50(5 m)^{49}+\binom{50}{2}(5 m)^{48} \pm \cdots \\ & \pm\binom{ 50}{47}(5 m)^{3}+\binom{50}{48}(5 m)^{2} \pm 50(5 m)+1 \end{aligned}$
All the terms except the final term have at least 3 factors of 5, so $N^{100}$ has remainder 1 upon division by 125 . Therefore there are only $(\text{B})\boxed{2}$ possible remainders: 0 and 1 .

$\textbf{OR}$
Let $\phi(n)$ be the number of positive integers less than $n$ that are relatively prime to $n$; this is Euler's totient function. Then $\phi(125)=5^{3}-5^{2}=100$. By Euler's Totient Theorem, if $a$ is not a multiple of 5 , then $a^{100} \equiv 1(\bmod 125)$. If $a$ is a multiple of 5 , then $a^{100} \equiv 0(\bmod 125)$. Therefore there are only $(\text{B})\boxed{2}$ possible remainders: 0 and 1 .

raw_content.title: A triangle in the coordinate plane has vertices $A\left(\log _{2} 1, \log _{2} 2\right), B\left(\log _{2} 3, \log _{2} 4\right)$, and $C\left(\log _{2} 7, \log _{2} 8\right)$. What is the area of $\triangle A B C$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
Circumscribe $\triangle A B C$ by rectangle $A G C D$, with $D$ on the $y$-axis, and project point $B$ onto $\overline{A G}$ and $\overline{C G}$, producing points $E$ and $F$, respectively, as shown in the figure below.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/c1d390071e8aba270244014889ea6216db95d807512ecc2e38124ae237be3cd8.jpg]

The area of rectangle $A G C D$ is $2 \log _{2} 7$, so the area of $\triangle A C G$ is $\log _{2} 7$. The requested area is

$\operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)=\operatorname{Area}(\triangle A C G)-\operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B E)-\operatorname{Area}(\triangle B C F)-\operatorname{Area}(B E G F) .$
Note that

$\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B E)=\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 3 \cdot 1=\log _{2} \sqrt{3}, \\ & \operatorname{Area}(\triangle B C F)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\log _{2} 7-\log _{2} 3\right) \cdot 1=\log _{2} \sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}, \text { and } \\ & \operatorname{Area}(B E G F)=\left(\log _{2} 7-\log _{2} 3\right) \cdot 1=\log _{2} \frac{7}{3} . \end{aligned}$
Therefore

$\begin{aligned} \text { Area }(\triangle A B C) & =\log _{2} 7-\log _{2} \sqrt{3}-\log _{2} \sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}-\log _{2} \frac{7}{3} \\ & =\log _{2}\left(\frac{7}{\sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{7}{3}} \cdot \frac{7}{3}}\right) \\ & =(\text{B})\boxed{\log _{2} \frac{3}{\sqrt{7}}} . \end{aligned}$
$\textbf{OR}$
The area of triangle $\triangle A B C$ is given by

$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{det}\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & \log _{2} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & \log _{2} 7 & 3 \end{array}\right] & =\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{det}\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & \log _{2} 3 & 0 \\ -2 & \log _{2} 7 & 0 \end{array}\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \operatorname{det}\left[\begin{array}{cc} -1 & \log _{2} 3 \\ -2 & \log _{2} 7 \end{array}\right] \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left(-\log _{2} 7+\log _{2} 9\right) \\ & =\log _{2} \frac{3}{\sqrt{7}} \end{aligned}$
The cross product of two vectors in the $x-y$ plane is a vector in the $z$ direction whose magnitude is twice the area of the triangle determined by the two vectors. The area of the triangle with vertices $A(0,1,0), B\left(\log _{2} 3,2,0\right)$, and $C\left(\log _{2} 7,3,0\right)$ is the $z$-component of

$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2}(B-A) & \times(C-A)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\log _{2} 3,1,0\right) \times\left(\log _{2} 7,2,0\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\left(1 \cdot 0-0 \cdot 2, \log _{2} 7 \cdot 0-\log _{2} 3 \cdot 0, \log _{2} 3 \cdot 2-1 \cdot \log _{2} 7\right) \\ & =\left(0,0, \log _{2} 3-\log _{2} \sqrt{7}\right)=\left(0,0, \log _{2} \frac{3}{\sqrt{7}}\right) . \end{aligned}$
Thus the area of the triangle is $(\text{B})\boxed{\log _{2} \frac{3}{\sqrt{7}}}$.

$\textbf{OR}$
Define the points $H(0,2), I(0,3)$, and $J\left(\log _{2} 3,3\right)$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/cdf55f5d8fb967893b86aa5a2b636e40931aaa788d19949c1782c76712a737ec.jpg]

Then $H B C I$ is a trapezoid, which can be decomposed into right triangle $\triangle C J B$ and rectangle HBJI. Because

$\log _{2} 3>\log _{2} \sqrt{7}=\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 7,$
point $B$ is to the right of line $A C$. Therefore

$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C) & =\operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B H)+\operatorname{Area}(H B C I)-\operatorname{Area}(\triangle A C I) \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 3+\frac{1}{2}\left(\log _{2} 7-\log _{2} 3\right)+\log _{2} 3-\log _{2} 7 \\ & =\log _{2} 3-\frac{1}{2} \log _{2} 7 \\ & =(\text{B})\boxed{\log _{2} \frac{3}{\sqrt{7}}} . \end{aligned}$

raw_content.title: Integers $a$ and $b$ are randomly chosen without replacement from the set of integers with absolute value not exceeding 10 . What is the probability that the polynomial $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+6$ has 3 distinct integer roots?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $r, s$, and $t$ be the roots of $x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+6$. Then

$x^{3}+a x^{2}+b x+6=(x-r)(x-s)(x-t)=x^{3}-(r+s+t) x^{2}+(r s+s t+t r) x-r s t,$
so $r s t=-6, r+s+t=-a$, and $r s+s t+t r=b$. The only triples of distinct integers that satisfy the first of these three equations are $(6,1,-1),(3,2,-1),(3,-2,1),(-3,2,1)$, and $(-3,-2,-1)$, together with their permutations. The corresponding values of $a$ and $b$ are $(-6,-1),(-4,1),(-2,-5)$, $(0,-7)$, and $(6,11)$, respectively.

Notice that these ordered pairs are distinct, but in only 4 of them do both $a$ and $b$ have absolute value not exceeding 10 . There are $21 \cdot 20$ equally likely choices for $a$ and $b$, so the required probability is $\frac{4}{21 \cdot 20}=(\text{C})\boxed{\frac{1}{105}}$.

raw_content.title:
Equilateral $\triangle A B C$ with side length 14 is rotated about its center by angle $\theta$, where $0<\theta \leq 60^{\circ}$, to form $\triangle D E F$. See the figure. The area of hexagon $A D B E C F$ is $91 \sqrt{3}$. What is $\tan \theta$ ?

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/d4124c3df42e608f6ce8558ef7dae82a9825ce0ac9002a79f520db10b5936a88.jpg]

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $O$ be the center of $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle D E F$, let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $\overline{A B}$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $\overline{A B}$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/a5256aa45879dd9b2be03ae46a2ff6cf9093138ec4af376be0c4e89953f19f23.jpg]

The condition $\theta \leq 60^{\circ}$ implies that $P$ lies on $\overline{A M}$ (as opposed to lying on $\overline{B M}$ ). Furthermore, $O$ is the center of the circle containing points $A, B$, and $D$, so by the Inscribed Angle Theorem $\angle D O A=2 \angle D B A$. It suffices to compute $\tan \angle D B A$ and then use the Double Angle Formula to obtain $\tan \theta$.

The area of $\triangle A B C$ is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \cdot 14^{2}=49 \sqrt{3}$. Because hexagon $A D B E C F$ consists of $\triangle A B C$ plus three copies of $\triangle A D B$, the area of $\triangle A D B$ is

$\frac{91 \sqrt{3}-49 \sqrt{3}}{3}=14 \sqrt{3} .$
This implies that $D P=2 \sqrt{3}$. Furthermore, $O M=\frac{7 \sqrt{3}}{3}$ and $O D=O A=2 \cdot O M=\frac{14 \sqrt{3}}{3}$. The Pythagorean Theorem yields

$\begin{aligned} M P & =\sqrt{O D^{2}-(O M+D P)^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{\left(\frac{14 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{13 \sqrt{3}}{3}\right)^{2}} \\ & =\sqrt{\frac{14^{2}-13^{2}}{3}}=\sqrt{\frac{27}{3}}=3 . \end{aligned}$
Finally, $B P=7+3=10$, so $\tan \angle D B A=\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{10}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{5}$ and

$\tan \theta=\tan (2 \angle D O B)=\frac{\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{5}}{1-\frac{3}{25}}=(\text{B})\boxed{\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{11}} .$
Note: The angle of rotation is about $38^{\circ}$.

raw_content.title: Suppose $A, B$, and $C$ are points in the plane with $A B=40$ and $A C=42$, and let $x$ be the length of the line segment from $A$ to the midpoint of $\overline{B C}$. Define a function $f$ by letting $f(x)$ be the area of $\triangle A B C$. Then the domain of $f$ is an open interval $(p, q)$, and the maximum value $r$ of $f(x)$ occurs at $x=s$. What is $p+q+r+s$ ?

solution_info.solution_info:
By the Triangle Inequality, $B C$ is between $40+42=82$ and $42-40=2$. The corresponding bounding values of $x$ are $p=42-\frac{40+42}{2}=1$ and $q=42-\frac{42-40}{2}=41$.\

The area of $\triangle A B C$ is maximized when $\angle B A C$ is a right angle, in which case the area is $r=$ $\frac{1}{2} \cdot 40 \cdot 42=840$, and the median to the hypotenuse has half the length of the hypotenuse, namely

$s=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{40^{2}+42^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{3364}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 58=29 .$
(This right triangle is the double of the $20-21-29$ right triangle.) The requested sum is $1+41+$ $840+29=(\text{C})\boxed{911}$.

Note: To compute the area of $\triangle A B C$ with $A B$ and $A C$ given, as a function of the length $x$ of the median to $\overline{B C}$, extend this median a distance $x$ beyond $\overline{B C}$ to a point $D$. Because diagonals $\overline{A D}$ and $\overline{B C}$ bisect each other, $A B D C$ is a parallelogram, and its area is twice the area of $\triangle A B C$ and also twice the area of $\triangle A B D$, whose side lengths are $A B=40, B D=A C=42$, and $A D=2 x$. This value can be computed by Heron's formula.

raw_content.title: The measures of the smallest angles of three different right triangles sum to $90^{\circ}$. All three triangles have side lengths that are primitive Pythagorean triples. Two of them are 3-4-5 and 5-12-13. What is the perimeter of the third triangle?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let the smallest angle of the 3-4-5 triangle have measure $\alpha$, the smallest angle of the $5-12-13$ triangle have measure $\beta$, and the smallest angle of the third triangle have measure $\gamma$. It is given that $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=90^{\circ}$, so $\cos (\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=0$. Expanding gives

$\begin{aligned} \cos (\alpha+\beta+\gamma) & =\cos (\alpha+\beta) \cos \gamma-\sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \gamma \\ & =(\cos \alpha \cos \beta-\sin \alpha \sin \beta) \cos \gamma-(\sin \alpha \cos \beta+\cos \alpha \sin \beta) \sin \gamma \\ & =\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma-\sin \alpha \sin \beta \cos \gamma-\sin \alpha \cos \beta \sin \gamma-\cos \alpha \sin \beta \sin \gamma \\ & =0 \end{aligned}$
Because $\sin \alpha=\frac{3}{5}, \cos \alpha=\frac{4}{5}, \sin \beta=\frac{5}{13}$, and $\cos \beta=\frac{12}{13}$,

$\begin{aligned} \cos (\alpha+\beta+\gamma) & =\frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{12}{13} \cos \gamma-\frac{3}{5} \cdot \frac{5}{13} \cos \gamma-\frac{3}{5} \cdot \frac{12}{13} \sin \gamma-\frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{5}{13} \sin \gamma \\ & =\frac{48}{65} \cos \gamma-\frac{15}{65} \cos \gamma-\frac{36}{65} \sin \gamma-\frac{20}{65} \sin \gamma \\ & =\frac{33}{65} \cos \gamma-\frac{56}{65} \sin \gamma \\ & =0 . \end{aligned}$
Therefore $33 \cos \gamma=56 \sin \gamma$, so $\tan \gamma=\frac{33}{56}$. Because 33 and 56 are relatively prime, perhaps they are the lengths of the two legs of the third triangle. Indeed, $33^{2}+56^{2}=1089+3136=4225=65^{2}$, and the perimeter of the triangle is $33+56+65=(\text{C})\boxed{154}$.

$\textbf{OR}$
Let $\alpha, \beta$, and $\gamma$ be as in the first solution. Using complex numbers in polar form, note that $4+3 i=$ $5 \mathrm{cis} \alpha$. Similarly, $12+5 i=13$ cis $\beta$. Multiplying these two quantities yields

$(4+3 i)(12+5 i)=33+56 i=65 \operatorname{cis}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\gamma\right),$
where the triangle with sides of length 33,56 , and 65 has angle $\gamma$ opposite the side of length 33 and angle $\frac{\pi}{2}-\gamma$ opposite the side of length 56 . Notice that

$\begin{aligned} (5 \operatorname{cis} \alpha) \cdot(13 \operatorname{cis} \beta) \cdot(65 \operatorname{cis} \gamma) & =(4+3 i)(12+5 i)(56+33 i) \\ & =65^{2} i \\ & =65^{2} \operatorname{cis}(\alpha+\beta+\gamma) \\ & =65^{2} \operatorname{cis} \frac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$
The third triangle has sides of length 33,56 , and 65 , and $33+56+65=(\text{C})\boxed{154}$.

Note: A fun fact about the $33-56-65$ triangle is that it is the smallest primitive Pythagorean triple that contains no prime values.

raw_content.title: Let $\triangle A B C$ be a triangle with integer side lengths and the property that $\angle B=2 \angle A$. What is the least possible perimeter of such a triangle?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $a, b$, and $c$ be the lengths of the sides opposite vertices $A, B$, and $C$, respectively. Note that $a<b$. Applying the Law of Sines in $\triangle A B C$, together with the identities $\sin B=\sin (2 A)=2 \sin A \cos A$ and

$\sin C=\sin (\pi-3 A)=\sin (3 A)=(\sin A)\left(-1+4 \cos ^{2} A\right)$
give

$\frac{\sin A}{a}=\frac{2 \sin A \cos A}{b}=\frac{\sin A\left(-1+4 \cos ^{2} A\right)}{c}$
Thus $\cos A=\frac{b}{2 a}$ and

$c=a\left(-1+4 \cos ^{2} A\right)=a\left(-1+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}\right)$
which simplifies to $b^{2}=a^{2}+a c$.

In looking for the triangle with least perimeter, it can be assumed that $a$ and $c$ are relatively prime, because otherwise a smaller triangle can be obtained by shrinking by a factor of $\operatorname{gcd}(a, c)$. Then $a$ and $a+c$ are relatively prime as well. Because $a(a+c)=b^{2}$, the numbers $a$ and $a+c$ must be squares, say $a=r^{2}$ and $a+c=s^{2}$, where $0<r<s$ and $\operatorname{gcd}(r, s)=1$. This gives $a=r^{2}, b=r s$, and $c=s^{2}-r^{2}$.

If $r=1$, then $b=s \geq 2$ and $c=s^{2}-1 \geq s+1$, a violation of the Triangle Inequality. If $r=2$, then the least perimeter will occur when $s=3$, with $a=2^{2}=4, b=2 \cdot 3=6$, and $c=3^{2}-2^{2}=5$. Greater values of $r$ lead to greater perimeters. The requested minimum perimeter is $4+6+5=(\text{C})\boxed{15}$.

Note: The 4-6-5 triangle has angle measures of approximately $\angle A=41.4^{\circ}, \angle B=82.8^{\circ}$, and $\angle C=55.8^{\circ}$. Triangles with the property that $\angle B=2 \angle A$ have been called $V U X$ triangles by Fitch Cheney in an article published in 1970 in The Mathematics Teacher.

raw_content.title: A right pyramid has regular octagon $A B C D E F G H$ with side length 1 as its base and apex $V$. Segments $\overline{A V}$ and $\overline{D V}$ are perpendicular. What is the square of the height of the pyramid?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $O$ be the center of the octagon, and let $r=A O$. As can be seen from the figure below, $A D=1+\sqrt{2}$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/84d817f784dece1ac6e7702ae6a6494b067e6b310172abef52519bd80eae9642.jpg]

Because $\triangle A V D$ is an isosceles right triangle,

$A V=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot A D=\frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{2}$
Applying the Law of Cosines to $\triangle A O H$ yields

$r^{2}+r^{2}=1^{2}+2 r^{2} \cos 45^{\circ}=1+r^{2} \sqrt{2}$
Thus $r^{2}(2-\sqrt{2})=1$ and

$r^{2}=\frac{1}{2-\sqrt{2}}=\frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{2}$
The Pythagorean Theorem applied to $\triangle V O A$ gives the requested square of the height of the pyramid:

$V O^{2}=A V^{2}-r^{2}=\left(\frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{2}=(\text{B})\boxed{\frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}}$
$\textbf{OR}$
Place the figure in a three-dimensional coordinate system with the center $O$ of the base of the pyramid at the origin, the octagon in the $x-y$ plane with positive $x$ coordinates for $A, B, C$, and $D$, the $y$-axis parallel to $\overline{A D}$, and apex $V(0,0, h)$ on the positive $z$-axis. See the figure.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/157d9f014652f5300537663811a0fadcddbcea978ef547159eb16a6a0dd7ec1a.jpg]

Then consider vectors

$\overrightarrow{O V}=\langle 0,0, h\rangle, \quad \overrightarrow{O A}=\left\langle\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}, 0\right\rangle, \quad \text { and } \quad \overrightarrow{O D}=\left\langle\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}, 0\right\rangle$
It follows that

$\overrightarrow{A V}=\overrightarrow{O V}-\overrightarrow{O A}=\left\langle-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}, h\right\rangle$
and

$\overrightarrow{D V}=\overrightarrow{O V}-\overrightarrow{O D}=\left\langle-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}, h\right\rangle$
Because $\overrightarrow{A V}$ and $\overrightarrow{D V}$ are perpendicular, their dot product is zero. Therefore

$0=\left\langle-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}, h\right\rangle \cdot\left\langle-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}, h\right\rangle=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{3+2 \sqrt{2}}{4}+h^{2}$
from which $h^{2}=(\text{B})\boxed{\frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}}$.

raw_content.title: What is the number of ordered triples $(a, b, c)$ of positive integers, with $a \leq b \leq c \leq 9$, such that there exists a (non-degenerate) triangle $\triangle A B C$ with an integer inradius for which $a, b$, and $c$ are the lengths of the altitudes from $A$ to $\overline{B C}, B$ to $\overline{A C}$, and $C$ to $\overline{A B}$, respectively? (Recall that the inradius of a triangle is the radius of the largest possible circle that can be inscribed in the triangle.)

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $x, y$, and $z$ be the lengths of $\overline{B C}, \overline{A C}$, and $\overline{A B}$, respectively. Let $r$ be the inradius of $\triangle A B C$. Then

$\operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)=\frac{1}{2} x a=\frac{1}{2} y b=\frac{1}{2} z c=\frac{1}{2}(x+y+z) r$
Therefore $x=\frac{2 \operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)}{a}, y=\frac{2 \operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)}{b}$, and $z=\frac{2 \operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)}{c}$, so

$\operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2 \operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)}{a}+\frac{2 \operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)}{b}+\frac{2 \operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)}{c}\right) r$
Dividing by $\operatorname{Area}(\triangle A B C)$ gives $\left(\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}\right) r=1$, so

$\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{r}$
Because $a, b, c \leq 9$, it follows that

$\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c} \geq \frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{9}=\frac{1}{3}$
implying $r \leq 3$. It is then possible to find the solutions $(a, b, c)$ by examining cases based on the value of $r$.

item If $r=1$, then, because $a \leq b \leq c$, either $a=2$ or $a=3$. If $a=2$, then $\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{2}$. Then, because $b \leq c$, either $b=3$ or $b=4$. If $b=3$, then $c=6$; and if $b=4$, then $c=4$. If $a=3$, then it must be that $b=c=3$. So the solutions in this case are $(2,3,6),(2,4,4)$, and $(3,3,3)$.

If $r=2$, then, because $a \leq b \leq c$, it follows that $a=3, a=4, a=5$, or $a=6$. If $a=3$, then $\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{6}$, which has no solutions because $\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{9}>\frac{1}{6}$. If $a=4$, then $\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{4}$. In this case, $b=c=8$ is the only solution. If $a=5$, then $\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{3}{10}$, which gives no solutions. If $a=6$, then it follows that $b=c=6$. So the solutions in this case are $(4,8,8)$ and $(6,6,6)$.

If $r=3$, then $(a, b, c)=(9,9,9)$ is the only solution because if $a<9$, then $c>9$.

Finally, the altitude lengths must be checked to ensure that these lengths give dimensions for a valid triangle. In the $(2,3,6)$ case, the side lengths of the triangles become $(3 t, 2 t, t)$ for some $t$, which does not form a triangle. In the $(2,4,4)$ and $(4,8,8)$ cases, the side lengths of the triangles become $(2 t, t, t)$ for some $t$, which again does not form a triangle. The rest of the cases, namely $(3,3,3)$, $(6,6,6)$, and $(9,9,9)$, do produce valid triangles because if all of the altitudes have length $h$, then it is possible to form an equilateral triangle with side length $\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3} h$. Thus there are $(\text{B})\boxed{3}$ ordered triples satisfying the given conditions.

raw_content.title: Pablo will decorate each of 6 identical white balls with either a striped or a dotted pattern, using either red or blue paint. He will decide on the color and pattern for each ball by flipping a fair coin for each of the 12 decisions he must make. After the paint dries, he will place the 6 balls in an urn. Frida will randomly select one ball from the urn and note its color and pattern. The events "the ball Frida selects is red" and "the ball Frida selects is striped" may or may not be independent, depending on the outcome of Pablo's coin flips. The probability that these two events are independent can be written as $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. What is $m$ ? (Recall that two events $A$ and $B$ are independent if $P(A$ and $B)=P(A) \cdot P(B)$.)

solution_info.solution_info:
There are $4^{6}$ ways to paint the balls, each equally likely. It remains to count the number of paintings for which the two given events are independent.

If all the balls are red, then $P($ red $)=1$ and the events are independent regardless of $P$ (striped). The same reasoning applies if all the balls are blue. This accounts for $2 \cdot 2^{6}=128$ paintings.

If 5 of the balls are red and $s$ balls are striped, then

$P(\text { red }) \cdot P(\text { striped })=\frac{5}{6} \cdot \frac{s}{6}$
On the other hand $P$ (red and striped) is one of the fractions $\frac{0}{6}, \frac{1}{6}, \frac{2}{6}, \frac{3}{6}, \frac{4}{6}$, or $\frac{5}{6}$, depending on how many red balls are striped. These are equal if and only if $s=0$ or $s=6$. There are $2 \cdot\binom{6}{5}=12$ ways for this to happen. A similar argument handles the case in which 5 balls are blue, giving 24 paintings in all.

Suppose 4 balls are red. In order for the two given events to be independent, the fraction of red balls that are striped must equal the fraction of blue balls that are striped. This happens when all the balls are striped, or none of them are striped, or 2 of the red balls and 1 of the blue balls are striped. There are $\binom{4}{2} \cdot\binom{2}{1}=12$ ways to choose the patterns in the last case, so this accounts for $\binom{6}{4} \cdot(1+1+12)=210$ situations. There are another 210 for which 2 balls are red.

Suppose 3 balls are red. Again, in order for the two given events to be independent, the fraction of red balls that are striped must equal the fraction of blue balls that are striped. This happens when $s$ red balls are striped and $s$ blue balls are striped, where $s \in\{0,1,2,3\}$. The calculation in this case is

$\binom{6}{3}\left(\binom{3}{0}^{2}+\binom{3}{1}^{2}+\binom{3}{2}^{2}+\binom{3}{3}^{2}\right)=20 \cdot 20=400$
In all there are $128+24+210+210+400=972$ cases in which the color and the pattern of the drawn ball are independent, so the required probability is

$\frac{972}{2^{12}}=\frac{243}{1024}$
and the requested numerator is $(\text{A})\boxed{243}$.

raw_content.title: A team of students is going to compete against a team of teachers in a trivia contest. The total number of students and teachers is $15$. Ash, a cousin of one of the students, wants to join the contest. If Ash plays with the students, the average age on that team will increase from $12$ to $14$. If Ash plays with the teachers, the average age on that team will decrease from $55$ to $52$. How old is Ash?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $s$ = number of students and $t$ = number of teachers. Then

$s + t = 15$
We can compute the average age of the students as follows:

$\frac{12s + A}{s + 1} = 14 \Rightarrow 12s + A = 14s + 14 \Rightarrow A = 2s + 14\tag{1}$
and the average age of the teachers:

$\frac{55t + A}{t + 1} = 52 \Rightarrow 55t + A = 52t + 52 \Rightarrow A = 52 - 3t\tag{2}$
Since we have $2$ values for $A$ in $(1)$ and $(2)$, we can equate them to get

$2s + 14 = 52 - 3t \Rightarrow 2s + 3t = 38\tag{3}$
From $s + t = 15$, $t=15-s$. We can substitute this into $(3)$ to get

$2s + 3(15 - s) = 38 \Rightarrow 2s + 45 - 3s = 38 \Rightarrow -s = -7 \Rightarrow s = 7, t=15-s=8$
Using $(1)$, we get

$A = 2s + 14 = 2(7) + 14 = 28$
which gives us an answer of $\boxed{\textbf{(A)~28}}$

raw_content.title:
Agnes writes the following four statements on a blank piece of paper.

At least one of these statements is true.

At least two of these statements are true.

At least two of these statements are false.

At least one of these statements is false.

Each statement is either true or false. How many false statements did Agnes write on the paper?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let the four statements be $S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4$ in order, and let $T$ be the number of true statements and $F$ the number of false ones, so $T+F=4$.

If $T = 0$, then all are false. But then $S_3$ says “at least two of these statements are false,” which would be true. Contradiction. So $T \ne 0$.

If $T = 4$, then all are true. But then $S_3$ (“at least two are false”) and $S_4$ (“at least one is false”) would both be false. Contradiction.

If $T = 2$, then $F = 2$. Then $S_3$ (“at least two are false”) is true, and $S_4$ (“at least one is false”) is also true, and $S_1$ (“at least one is true”) is true as well. That gives at least three true statements, so $T \ge 3$, a contradiction.

If $T = 1$, then $F = 3$. Then $S_1$ (“at least one is true”) must be true. Since $F = 3$, $S_3$ (“at least two are false”) is also true, giving at least two true statements, so $T \ge 2$, a contradiction.

The only remaining possibility is

$T=3,\quad F=1.$
Indeed, if three statements are true and one is false, then $S_1$, $S_2$, and $S_4$ are true, and $S_3$ is false, which is consistent.

Therefore, the number of false statements Agnes wrote is $\boxed{\textbf{(B)~1}}$.

raw_content.title: Six chairs are arranged around a round table. Two students and two teachers randomly select four of the chairs to sit in. What is the probability that the two students will sit in two adjacent chairs and the two teachers will also sit in two adjacent chairs?

solution_info.solution_info:
If we look around the circle, we can seat the people in $6\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot 3$ total ways (with full distinguishability). However, if our condition is met, we will first seat the teachers in $6\cdot 2$ ways (the second teacher must occupy one of the two adjacent spots). Then, the remaining students can choose their seats in $6$ ways (there are $4$ chairs left, so there are $3$ pairs of adjacent seats, and $2$ orders for them to sit in). Thus our overall probaility is

$\dfrac{6\cdot 2\cdot 6}{6\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot 3}=\dfrac 15$
which gives us an answer of $\boxed{\textbf{(B)}~\frac{1}{5}}$

raw_content.title: In a certain alien world, the maximum running speed $v$ of an organism is dependent on its number of toes $n$ and number of eyes $m$. The relationship can be expressed as $v=k n^{a} m^{b}$ centimeters per hour, where $k,a,b$ are integer constants. In a population where all organisms have $5$ toes, $\log v=4+2\log m$; and in a population where all organisms have $25$ eyes, $\log v=4+4\log n$ (base $10$). What is $k+a+b?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Note that $\log v = \log k + \log n^a + \log m^b = \log v = \log k + a\log n + b\log m$.

Plugging into the first equation with $n=5$ and the second equation with $m = 25$:

$\log k + a\log 5 + b\log m = 4 + 2\log m \\ \log k + a\log n + b\log 25 = 4 + 4\log n$
As the equations must be true no matter how $n$ and $m$ vary, the $\log n$ and $\log m$ terms must cancel out in each equation respectively. This gives $a=4$ and $b=2$.

Substituting into the first equation gives:

$\log k + 4\log 5 + 2\log m = 4 + 2\log m \rightarrow \log k = 4 - 4\log 5 = 4(\log 10 - \log 5) = 4\log 2 = \log 16$
So $k + a + b$ = $16 + 4 + 2$ = $\boxed{\textbf{(C)~22}}$.

raw_content.title: Pentagon $ABCDE$ is inscribed in a circle, and $\angle BEC=\angle CED=30^{\circ}$. Let $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BD}$ intersect at point $F$, and suppose that $AB=9$ and $AD=24$. What is $BF?$

solution_info.solution_info:
[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/f2138ef8a8c12dae74486afdf28ac439dc1493aca25eb72f60e5272d8751b8c1.png]

Note that as $\angle BEC$ and $\angle CED$ are angles inscribed in arcs $\overset{\frown}{BC}$ and $\overset{\frown}{CD}$, so thus $\angle BAC=\angle CAD=30^\circ$.

This means that $AC$ is an angle bisector of $\angle BAD$, so we can apply the Angle Bisector Theorem. Also note that

$\angle BAD=180^\circ-BCD=180^\circ-120^\circ=60^\circ$
By the Law of Cosines,

$BD^2=AD^2+AB^2-2\cdot AB\cdot AD\cdot\cos\angle BAD=9^2+24^2-2\cdot 9\cdot 24\cos 60^\circ=441$
so $BD=21$. Then, by the Angle Bisector Theorem,

$BF=\dfrac{AB}{AB+AD}\cdot BD=\dfrac 9{9+24}\cdot 21=\dfrac{63}{11}$
leading to an answer of $\boxed{\textbf{(E)}~\dfrac{63}{11}}$.

raw_content.title: Let $w=2+i$. What real number $r$ has the property that $r$, $w$, and $w^{2}$ are three collinear points in the complex plane?

solution_info.solution_info:
We need $2+i$,$(2+i)^2 = 3 + 4i$ and $r$ to be collinear in the complex plane, which is equivalent to ensuring that the points $(2,1),(3,4),(r,0)$ are collinear.

Equating on slopes:

$\dfrac{4-1}{3-2} = \dfrac{0-4}{r-3} \rightarrow 3(r-3) = -4 \rightarrow r = \dfrac{5}{3} \rightarrow {\color{OliveGreen}\boxed{{\textbf{(E)}}}}.$

raw_content.title:
In the figure shown below, major arc $\widehat{AD}$ and minor arc $\widehat{BC}$ have the same center $O$. Also, $A$ lies between $O$ and $B$, and $D$ lies between $O$ and $C$. Major arc $\widehat{AD}$, minor arc $\widehat{BC}$, and each of the two segments $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ have length $2\pi$.

What is the distance from $O$ to $A?$

$r_2\theta = 2\pi$
$r_2-r_1 = 2\pi$
Substituting $r_2 = r_1 + 2\pi$ into $r_2\theta = 2\pi$ gives $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{r_1 + 2\pi}$. Substituting this into the first equation:

raw_content.title: The orthocenter of a triangle is the concurrent intersection of the three (possibly extended) altitudes. What is the sum of the coordinates of the orthocenter of the triangle whose vertices are $A(2,31)$, $B(8,27)$, and $C(18,27)?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Consider the altitude from $A$ to $BC$. This line has equation $x = 2$.

Consider the altitude from $C$ to $AB$. The slope of this line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of $AB$.

The slope of $AB = \dfrac{27-31}{8-2} = -\dfrac{2}{3}$, which means the slope of $AB$ is $\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Thus the equation of the altitude through $C$ is:

$y-27 = \dfrac{3}{2}(x-18)$ and plugging in $x=2$ gives $y = 3$, so $x+y$ = $\boxed{\textbf{(A)~5}}$

raw_content.title:
The harmonic mean of a collection of numbers is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals of the numbers in the collection. For example, the harmonic mean of $4,4,5$ is

$\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{5}\right)}=\dfrac{30}{7}.$
What is the harmonic mean of all the real roots of the $4050^{\text{th}}$ degree polynomial

$\prod_{k=1}^{2025}\left(kx^{2}-4x-3\right)=\left(x^{2}-4x-3\right)\left(2x^{2}-4x-3\right)\cdots\left(2025x^{2}-4x-3\right)?$

solution_info.solution_info:
The sum of the reciprocals of the roots of $kx^2 - 4x - 3$ for some $k$ is $\dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2} = \dfrac{r_1 + r_2}{r_1r_2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{4}{k}}{\dfrac{-3}{k}} = -\dfrac{4}{3}$.

Therefore, the sum of all the reciprocals of the roots of the polynomial is $-\dfrac{4}{3} * 2025$ and the average is then $\dfrac{-\dfrac{4}{3}*2025}{4050} = \dfrac{-2}{3}$.

Reciprocating gives our answer of $-\dfrac{3}{2} \rightarrow \boxed{\textbf{(B)}}$

raw_content.title: Let $C=\{1,2,3,\ldots,13\}$. Let $N$ be the greatest integer such that there exists a subset of $C$ with $N$ elements that does not contain five consecutive integers. Suppose $N$ integers are chosen at random from $C$ without replacement. What is the probability that the chosen elements do not include five consecutive integers?

solution_info.solution_info:
If we skip only one element from $C$, then there will be at least $5$ elements greater than the skipped one or $5$ elements less.

Therefore we must skip $2$ elements and it is easy to see that this is possible e.g. skipping $5$ and $10$.

Now, we must compute the number of ways to delete $2$ elements while ensuring no $5$ numbers are consecutive.

There are only $3$ ways to do this - skipping $\{5,10\}, \{4,9\},$ or $\{5,9\}$ for a probability of $\dfrac{3}{{13 \choose 2}} = \dfrac{1}{26}\rightarrow \boxed{\textbf{(D)}}$.

raw_content.title:
Points $F, G,$ and $H$ are collinear with $G$ between $F$ and $H$. The ellipse with foci at $G$ and $H$ is internally tangent to the ellipse with foci at $F$ and $G$, as shown below.

The two ellipses have the same eccentricity $e$, and the ratio of their areas is $2025$. What is $e?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $K$ be the intersection (or tangency) point of the two circles.

Note that the ellipses are similar - in fact, consider the dilation at $K$ that maps the larger ellipse to the smaller ellipse. It must preserve foci, so it must map $F$ to $G$ and $G$ to $H$.

This means that

$\dfrac{FK}{GK}=\dfrac{GK}{HK}$
or $FK\cdot HK=GK^2$.

If we let $c$ and $a$ be defined as in the problem for the larger ellipse, we get $FK=c+a$ and $GK=c-a$.

Furthermore, since the ellipses are similar, $HK$ is a scaled down version of $GK$, with ratio $\sqrt{2025}=45$ (the ratio of areas of similar figures is the square of the ratio of their lengths).

Hence, we get

$FK\cdot GK\cdot\dfrac 1{45}=GK^2$
or

$c+a=45(c-a)$
so $\dfrac ca=\dfrac{22}{23}$, or $\boxed{\textbf{(D)}}$.

raw_content.title: Triangle $\triangle ABC$ has side lengths $AB=80$, $BC=45$, and $AC=75$. The bisector of $\angle B$ and the altitude to side $\overline{AB}$ intersect at point $P$. What is $BP?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $C$ to $\overline{AB}$, and let $P$ be the intersection of $BD$ (the bisector of $\angle B$) with $\overline{CD}$. We find $AD$ and $BD$ using the Pythagorean theorem.

From right triangles $ADC$ and $BDC$,

$AC^{2}=AD^{2}+CD^{2},$
$BC^{2}=BD^{2}+CD^{2}.$
From above, we get:

$AC^{2}-BC^{2}=AD^{2}-BD^{2}=(AD-BD)(AD+BD).$
$\begin{aligned} AD+BD=AB=80, AC=75, \, BC=45,&\implies (75^{2}-45^{2})=80(AD-BD)\\ &\implies (75-45)(75+45)=80(AD-BD)\\ &\implies 30\cdot120=80(AD-BD)\\ &\implies AD-BD=45.\\ \end{aligned}$
Solving

$\begin{cases} AD+BD=80,\\ AD-BD=45, \end{cases}$
we get

$AD=\dfrac{125}{2}, \; BD=\dfrac{35}{2}.$
We find $CD$ by applying the Pythagorean theorem in $\triangle BDC$.

$CD=\sqrt{BC^{2}-BD^{2}} =\sqrt{45^{2}-\left(\dfrac{35}{2}\right)^{2}} =\sqrt{\dfrac{6875}{4}} =\dfrac{25}{2}\sqrt{11}.$
We use the Angle Bisector Theorem in $\triangle BCD$ to find $DP$. Since $BP$ bisects $\angle B$,

$\dfrac{DP}{PC}=\dfrac{BD}{BC} =\dfrac{\dfrac{35}{2}}{45} =\dfrac{7}{18} \;\Rightarrow\; DP=\dfrac{7}{25} \, CD.$
Hence,

$DP=\dfrac{7}{25}\cdot \dfrac{25}{2}\sqrt{11} =\dfrac{7\sqrt{11}}{2}.$
Now, we can again use the Pythagorean Theorem in $\triangle BDP$ to find $BP$.

$BP^{2}=BD^{2}+DP^{2} =\left(\dfrac{35}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(\dfrac{7\sqrt{11}}{2}\right)^{2} =\dfrac{1225}{4}+\dfrac{539}{4} =\dfrac{1764}{4}=441.$
so $BP={\boxed{\textbf{(D)~21}}}$

raw_content.title: The polynomial $(z+i)(z+2i)(z+3i)+10$ has three roots in the complex plane. What is the area of the triangle formed by these roots?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $x = z+2i$. Then the polynomial becomes $(x-i)x(x+i)+10 = 0 \rightarrow x^{3} + x + 10 = 0$. We spot that $-2$ is a root of this polynomial:

$x^{3} + x + 10 = (x+2)(x^{2}-2x+5)$
The three solutions for $x$ are then $-2,1+2i,1-2i$. Since shifting the solution back to $z$ is a translation of the points, we can just compute the area directly. raw_content.title: How many ordered triples $(x,y,z)$ of distinct nonnegative integers $\le 8$ satisfy $xy>z,$ $zx>y,$ and $yz>x?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Without loss of generality, assume $x < y < z$. Now we count the complement, that is how many triples result in $xy \leq z$ or $xz \leq y$ or $yz \leq x$. $yz \leq x$ is impossible and $xz \leq y$ only holds if $x = 0$, which would imply $xy \leq z$ anyways. Therefore, it suffices to compute the number of triples where $xy < z$.

$\textbf{Case 1}$: $x = 0$. There are $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ possibilities for $y$ and $z$.

$\textbf{Case 2}$: $x = 1$. If $x = 1$, for some given $y$ then, $z \in \{y+1,y+2,\ldots,y+8\}$ all result in $xy < z$. There are $8-y$ options in the set, so summing across all $y$ gives:

$\sum_{y=2}^{7} 8-y = 21$
$\textbf{Case 3}$: $x = 2$. We see that $y = 3$, $z \geq 6$ and $y=4$, $z=8$ work for $4$ possibilities.

$\textbf{Case 4}$: $x\geq 3$. If $x \geq 3$, then we are guaranteed $xy > z$. This gives $0$ possibilities.

There are $\binom{9}{3}$ ways to pick $x$, $y$, and $z$ in increasing order for a total of $6(84-28-21-4) = \boxed{\textbf{(C)~186}}$ ordered triples.

raw_content.title:
There is a unique ordered triple $(a,k,m)$ of nonnegative integers such that

$\dfrac{4^{a}+4^{a+k}+4^{a+2k}+\cdots+4^{a+mk}}{2^{a}+2^{a+k}+2^{a+2k}+\cdots+2^{a+mk}}=964.$
What is $a+k+m?$

solution_info.solution_info:
We can use the geometric series formula to write:

$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4^{a}+4^{a+k}+4^{a+2 k}+\cdots+4^{a+m k}}{2^{a}+2^{a+k}+2^{a+2 k}+\cdots+2^{a+m k}} &= \dfrac{4^a\left(\dfrac{4^{(m + 1)k} - 1}{4^k - 1}\right)}{2^a\left(\dfrac{2^{(m + 1)k} - 1}{2^k - 1}\right)} \\ &= 2^a \cdot \dfrac{2^{(m + 1)k} + 1}{2^k + 1} \end{aligned}$
Note that $\dfrac{2^{(m + 1)k} + 1}{2^k + 1}$ is odd, so $a = 2$, since $964 = 2^{2} \cdot 241$. Hence:

$\dfrac{2^{(m + 1)k} + 1}{2^k + 1} = 241$
Note that $241 = 2^{8} - 2^{4} + 1$, so $(m + 1)k = 12$ and $k = 4$. Hence, we have $a = 2$, $m = 2$, and $k = 4$, which yields a final answer of $\boxed{\textbf{(A)}~8}$.

$\textbf{Remark.}$ Note that the last part can be formalized with $\text{Zsigmondy's Theorem}$. $2^{(m+1)k}+1$ will have a unique prime divisor not dividing $241$ or $2^{k}+1$ for any $(m+1)k>12$, hence $(m+1)k\leq 12$. It's easy to see $2^{m+1}k\geq 3\cdot 241=723$, so $(m+1)k=10,11,12$, of which only $k=4,m=2$ works.

raw_content.title: Call a positive integer fair if no digit is used more than once, it has no $0$s, and no digit is adjacent to two greater digits. For example, $196$, $23,$ and $12463$ are fair, but $1546$, $320,$ and $34321$ are not fair. How many fair positive integers are there?

solution_info.solution_info:
$\textbf{Claim.}$ The smallest digit must appear on one of its ends.

$\textbf{Proof.}$ Let $S$ be a set of digits, and let $s = \min S$ denote the smallest element of the set.

Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that $s$ is not positioned at either end of a fair arrangement.

Then $s$ would have two neighbors, both of which must be greater than $s$, since it is the smallest digit in $S$.

This violates the definition of a fair arrangement, which prohibits any digit from being adjacent to two larger digits.

Therefore, the smallest digit must always occupy one of the end positions. This completes the proof of the claim.

Once the smallest digit has been placed at an end, we must verify that the remaining digits continue to form a fair arrangement.

This is achieved by repeating the same logic on the reduced set $S \setminus \{s\}$, where we again identify and place the smallest remaining digit at one of the ends.

To visualize this process, imagine constructing the arrangement step by step.

Begin with the smallest digit, then sequentially insert each next-smallest digit at either the left end or the right end of the current sequence.

If there are $k$ digits in total, the first digit can be placed in either end position ($2$ options).

At each subsequent step, the next-smallest digit can again be placed on either the left or right end.

This continues until all but one digit is placed, leaving a single remaining position for the final digit.

Hence, for a set $S$ with $k$ digits, the total number of fair arrangements is

$2^{k-1}.$
Now, we will count all fair integers. Choose the $k$ digits (no $0$) in $\binom{9}{k}$ ways and arrange them fairly in $2^{k-1}$ ways. Summing over $k=1,\dots,9$,

$T=\sum_{k=1}^{9}\binom{9}{k}2^{k-1} =\binom{9}{1}2^{0}+\binom{9}{2}2^{1}+\cdots+\binom{9}{9}2^{8}.$
Multiply both sides by $2$ and add $\binom{9}{0}$:

$2T+\binom{9}{0}=\sum_{k=1}^{9}\binom{9}{k}2^{k}+\binom{9}{0} =\sum_{k=0}^{9}\binom{9}{k}2^{k}=(1+2)^{9}=3^{9}.$
Thus

$2T+1=3^{9} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T=\dfrac{3^{9}-1}{2}.$
Since $3^{9}=19683$, the total number of fair positive integers is

$T=\dfrac{19683-1}{2}= \boxed{\textbf{(C)~9841}}$

raw_content.title: Polynomials $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ each have degree $3$ and leading coefficient $1$, and their roots are all elements of $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. The function $f(x) = \tfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ has the property that there exist real numbers $a < b < c < d$ such that the set of all real numbers $x$ such that $f(x) \leq 0$ consists of the closed interval $[a,b]$ together with the open interval $(c,d)$. How many ordered pairs of polynomials $(P, Q)$ are possible?

solution_info.solution_info:
None of the answer choices on the official test (which asked for the number of possible functions $f(x)$) were correct, but choice E would be correct if this problem asked for the number of pairs of functions $(P(x), Q(x))$.

Let $R(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$. Since $R(x) \leq 0$ on $[a, b]$ but not for values slightly less than $a$ or slightly more than $b$, $P(x) = 0$ at $x = a$ and $x = b$. Therefore, $P(x) = (x-a)(x-b)(x-r)$ for some $r \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$.

Since $R(x) \leq 0$ on $(c, d)$ but not at $x = c$ or $x = d$, $R(x)$ is not continuous at $x = c$ or $x = d$. Therefore, $R(x)$ must be undefined at $x = c$ and $x = d$, that is, $Q(x) = 0$ at $x = c$ and $x = d$. So $Q(x) = (x-c)(x-d)(x-s)$ for some $s \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$.

Therefore, $R(x) = \frac{(x-a)(x-b)(x-r)}{(x-c)(x-d)(x-s)}$. Notice that $\frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(x-c)(x-d)} \leq 0$ only on $[a, b]$ and $(c, d)$. Therefore, $\frac{x-r}{x-s}$ must be nonnegative for all $x \notin \{a, b, c, d, r, s\}$. This only happens if $r = s$.

Thus $R(x) = \frac{(x-a)(x-b)(x-r)}{(x-c)(x-d)(x-r)}$, which is the same as $\frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(x-c)(x-d)}$ except that it is undefined at $x = r$. Thus $R(x)$ satisfies the desired property as long as $r \notin [a, b] \cup (c, d)$.

Note that each quintuple $(a, b, c, d, r)$ defines a unique pair of functions $(P(x), Q(x))$.

If $(a, b, c, d) = (1, 2, 3, 4)$, $r$ can be $3$, $4$, or $5$.

If $(a, b, c, d) = (1, 2, 3, 5)$, $r$ can be $3$ or $5$.

If $(a, b, c, d) = (1, 2, 4, 5)$, $r$ can be $3$, $4$, or $5$.

If $(a, b, c, d) = (1, 3, 4, 5)$, $r$ can be $4$ or $5$.

If $(a, b, c, d) = (2, 3, 4, 5)$, $r$ can be $1$, $4$, or $5$.

Therefore, there are $\boxed{(\textbf{E})\ 13}$ possible pairs of functions $(P(x), Q(x))$.

For any function $g(x)$, define a real number $t$ as a toggling point for $g(x)$ if there exists a sequence $t_1 < t_2 < ... < t_N$, with the understanding that $t_0 = -\infty$ and $t_{N+1} = \infty$, such that

$t = t_k$ for some $1 \leq k \leq N$,

$g(x)$ is of the same sign (either always positive or always negative) on each interval $(t_j, t_{j+1})$, for $j=0, ..., N$, and

$g(x)$ has opposite signs on $(t_{k-1}, t_k)$ and $(t_k, t_{k+1})$.
We call these open intervals $(t_j, t_{j+1})$ ($j=0, ..., N$) the bands of $g(x)$.

The polynomial $P(x)$ has no toggling point outside of $D$, and $Q(x)$ has no toggling point outside of $E$. Now in our problem, $f(x)$ has exactly 4 toggling points: $a, b, c, d$. Our task is to see how these four points are related to the sets $D$ and $E$.

Lemma. At each toggling point $t$ for $f(x)$,

either $P(t)=0$ or $Q(t)=0$ (or both);

if the multiplicities of the root $t$ of $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are $m$ and $n$, respectively, then $m-n$ is odd.
Proof. (1) if both $P(t)$ and $Q(t)$ are nonzero, then $t$ belongs to a band of $P(x)$ and a band of $Q(x)$. Taking the intersection between these two bands, we get an open interval on which $f(x)$ has the same sign as $f(t)$. Thus $t$ cannot be a toggling point of $f(x)$.

(2) If $m$ is odd, there are real numbers $r, s$, with $r<t<s$, such that $P(x)$ has the same sign on $(r,t)$ and has the opposite sign on $(t, s)$. If $m$ is even, there are real numbers $r, s$, with $r<t<s$, such that $P(x)$ has the same sign on $(r,t)$ and on $(t,s)$. Similar statements can be made of $Q(x)$, having intervals $(u, t)$ and $(t, v)$ so that $Q(t)$ is of the same sign on $(u,t)$, and of either a different or the same sign on $(t, v)$, depending on the parity of $n$. If both $m$ and $n$ are odd or both $m$ and $n$ are even, then $P(t)/Q(t)$ is of the same sign on the interval $(\max\{r, u\}, t)$ and $(t, \min\{s, v\})$, so $t$ cannot be a toggling point for $f(x)$.

Solution to the problem.
Since $a$ is a toggling point for $f(x)$, either $P(a)=0$ or $Q(a)=0$, or both. But since $f(a)$ is defined, we have $Q(a)\neq 0$, so $P(a)=0$. The same can be said of $b$, so $P(b)=0$. The multiplicities of $a$ and $b$ must be $1$. Otherwise, point (2) of the Lemma would require the multiplicity of one of them to be at least $3$, but $P(x)$ is only cubic.

$c$ is a toggling point for $f(x)$, so either $P(c)=0$ or $Q(c)=0$, or both. But if $Q(c)\neq 0$, we have $f(c)=0$, violating the condition. So $Q(c)=0$. Similarly, $Q(d)=0$. Concerning their multiplicities, point (2) of the Lemma gives us three cases, given that $Q(x)$ is only cubic:

(a) $c$ is a single root of $Q(x)$, $P(c)\neq 0$, $d$ is a double root of $Q(x)$ and a single root of $P(x)$;

(b) switching the roles of $c$ and $d$;

(c) both $c$ and $d$ are single roots of $Q(x)$, and $Q(x)$ has a single root $e$ other than $c$ and $d$.

Case (a) provides functions in the form of $\frac{(x-a)(x-b)(x-d)}{(x-c)(x-d)^2}$. There are 5 of them because there are 5 ways to choose $a, b, c, d$ from the set $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$.

Case (c) requires that $P(e)=0$, because if $P(e)\neq 0$ then $e$ becomes an extra toggling point for $f(x)$. So this case provides functions in the form of $\frac{(x-a)(x-b)(x-e)}{(x-c)(x-d)(x-e)}$. But since $f(e)$ is undefined, we need to make sure that $e$ does not fall into $[a,b]$ or $(c,d)$. So $e$ can be $1, 3, 5$. In all these cases, we also have $f(e) = \frac{(e-a)(e-b)}{(e-c)(e-d)} > 0$, satisfying the conditions. That's 3 more functions.

So the total number of functions is $5 + 3 = \boxed{8}$.

For the condition $f(x)\le 0 \iff x\in [a,b]\cup(c,d)$, $f$ must change sign at $a, b, c,$ and $d$. The key trick is that a rational function can only change sign through zeroes or discontinuities. Since both $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are monic cubic polynomials, $f(x) \to 1$ as $x \to \pm\infty$. This means $f(x)$ is $+$ for large $|x|$. The required sign pattern must therefore be:
$f(x): \quad +\underset{ a }{ [ }-\underset{ b }{ ] }+\underset{ c }{ ( }-\underset{ d }{ ) }+$

For the interval to be closed, $[a, b]$, we must have $f(a) = 0$ and $f(b) = 0$. This implies $P(a) = P(b) = 0$ and, critically, $Q(a) \neq 0$ and $Q(b) \neq 0$ to avoid discontinuity.

For the interval to be open, $(c, d)$, the function must be undefined at the endpoints: if $f(c)$ were defined, by the intermediate value theorem $f(c)=0$, violating the condition. This implies $Q(c) = 0$ and $Q(d) = 0$. Note that $P(c),P(d)$ could be $0$, as $\frac{0}{0}$ remains undefined.

From this, we conclude that $a, b, c, d\in \{ 1,2,3,4,5 \}$. Let the remaining root in be $t$, so $\{ 1,2,3,4,5 \}=\{ a,b,c,d,t \}$.

Let $p_i, q_i\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ be the multiplicities of a root $i=1,2,3,4,5$ in $P(x),Q(x)$, respectively, e.g. $P(x)=(x-1)^{p_{1}}(x-2)^{p_{2}}(x-3)^{p_{3}}(x-4)^{p_{4}}(x-5)^{p_{5}}$. Let the multiplicity in $f(x)$ at $i$ be $m_i = p_i - q_i$. A sign change occurs at $i$ if and only if $m_i$ is odd.

The sign changes at $a, b, c, d$. Thus, $m_a, m_b, m_c, m_d$ must all be odd.

The sign does not change at $t$. Thus, $m_t$ must be even.

From the root analysis, $q_a = 0 \implies m_a=p_{a}-q_{a} = p_a$ is odd. Similarly, $p_b$ is odd. Since $\deg(P) = \sum p_i = 3$, and $p_a, p_b\ge 1$ are odd, $m_{a}=m_{b}=p_{a}=p_{b}=1$. This forces the roots of $P(x)$ to be distinct: $\{a, b, k\}$ for some $k \in \{ 1,2,3,4,5 \} \setminus \{a, b\}$ with $p_{k}=1$.

We already distributed $2$ roots for $P$ and $Q$ each, so there is $1$ left to give. Our constraints give $p_{c}+p_{d}+p_{t}=1$, $p_{c},p_{d},p_{t}\in \{ 0,1 \}$ and $q_{t}\in \{0,1\}$, $q_{c}, q_{d}\in \{ 1,2 \}$. We can make some inferences:

$p_{c}\in \{ 0,1 \}$, $q_c \in \{ 1,2 \}$, $m_c=p_{c}-q_{c} \in \{ -2,-1,0 \}$. Since $m_c$ is odd, $m_{c} = -1$. Similarly, $m_{d}=-1$.

$p_{t}\in \{ 0,1 \}$, $q_{t}\in \{ 0,1 \}$, $m_{t}=p_{t}-q_{t}\in \{ -1,0,1 \}$. Since $m_{t}$ is even, $m_{t}=0$.

At this point, we have $(m_{a},m_{b},m_{c},m_{d},m_{t})=(1,1,-1,-1,0)$. But this is exactly the distribution of multiplicities of $\frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(x-c)(x-d)}$, which is forced from the beginning. Thus, the remaining multiplicity of each of $P$ and $Q$ must cancel into a single bin to create net multiplicity $0=1-1$, yielding

$f(x)=\frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(x-c)(x-d)}\cdot \frac{x-k}{x-k}$
where $k=c,d,t$, and this creates a hole if there isn't one already. However, the problem is that if there is already a hole (i.e. $k=c,d$), then this factor $\frac{x-k}{x-k}$ changes nothing as $f$ was already undefined at $x=k$, so while it gives a different pair of polynomials, it does not provide a new function $f$.

Cases $k=c,d$ are symmetric:

WLOG, let $k=c$, and choosing $t=1,2,3,4,5$ determines the remaining $1\le a<b<c<d \le 5$. Each $t$ creates a unique pair of polynomials, so there are $2\cdot \binom{5}{1}=10$ pairs of polynomials. However, as established, puncturing a hole again on $k=c,d$ does nothing:
$f(x)=\frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(x-c)(x-d)}\cdot \frac{x-c}{x-c}=\frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(x-c)(x-d)}\cdot \frac{x-d}{x-d}$
So each $t$ creates exactly one new function regardless of whether $k=c$ or $k=d$, i.e. there are only $5$ new functions.

Case $k=t$:

Sketching a quick diagram for $(\text{sign pattern of }f)$, $t$ cannot puncture $[a,b]$ nor $(c,d)$, meaning it must lie outside them. All other cases cases do work, since you can puncture $+$ intervals without affecting $-$ intervals.
$\begin{cases} t,[a,b],(c,d) \\ [a,b],t,(c,d) \\ [a,b],(c,d),t \end{cases}$
Hence, there are $3$ valid choices of $t$.

In total, there are $10+3=\boxed{ \textbf{(E)}~13 }$ ordered pairs of polynomials $(P,Q)$ but only $\boxed{ 8 }$ different functions created by $f=\frac{P}{Q}$.

raw_content.title: What is the value of $i(i-1)(i-2)(i-3)$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Consider the polynomial:

$P(x) = x(x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3) = x^4 - 6x^3 + 11x^2 - 6x$
Then $P(i) = i(i - 1)(i - 2)(i - 3) = 1 + 6i - 11 - 6i = -10$, so the answer is $\boxed{{\textbf{(D)~-10}}}$.

Alternate Solution:

We can manually multiply everything out as follows:

$\begin{aligned} i(i - 1)(i - 2)(i - 3) &= (-1 - i)(i - 2)(i - 3) \\ &= (3 + i)(i - 3) = -10 \end{aligned}$
which yields the same answer as before.

raw_content.title: The value of the two-digit number $\underline{a} \ \underline{b}$ in base seven equals the value of the two-digit number $\underline{b} \ \underline{a}$ in base nine. What is $a+b?$

solution_info.solution_info:
The base-$7$ number $\overline{ab}_7$ equals the base-$9$ number $\overline{ba}_9$:

$7a + b = 9b + a.$
Thus

$7a + b = 9b + a \;\Longrightarrow\; 6a = 8b \;\Longrightarrow\; 3a = 4b.$
So $a = 4k$, $b = 3k$ for some integer $k$. Since $a,b$ are digits in base $7$, we require $1 \le a,b \le 6$. The only possibility is $k=1$, giving $(a,b) = (4,3)$.

Hence

$a + b = 4 + 3 = \color{OliveGreen}\boxed{{\textbf{(A)~7}}}.$

raw_content.title: Positive integers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the equation $57x+22y=400$. What is the least possible value of $x+y?$

solution_info.solution_info: We need $57x \equiv 400 \pmod{22}$, which is equivalent to $13x \equiv 4 \pmod{22}$. Since $13^{-1} \equiv 17 \pmod{22}$, we have $x \equiv 2 \pmod{22}$. Because $x$ and $y$ are positive integers, we must have $x = 2$, which corresponds to $y = 13$. Hence, there is only one possible value of $x + y$, namely $2 + 13 = 15$, so the answer is $\boxed{{\textbf{(E)~15}}}$.

raw_content.title:
What is the value of

$\sum_{n=2}^{255}\frac{\log_{2}\!\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)}{\left(\log_{2}n\right)\left(\log_{2}(n+1)\right)}\ ?$

solution_info.solution_info:
We can write:

$\begin{aligned} \sum_{n = 2}^{255} \dfrac{\log_2\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{n}\right)}{(\log_2 n)(\log_2 (n + 1))} &= \sum_{n = 2}^{255} \dfrac{\log_2(n + 1) - \log_2(n)}{\log_2(n) \cdot \log_2(n + 1)} \\ &= \sum_{n = 2}^{255} \left(\dfrac{1}{\log_2(n)} - \dfrac{1}{\log_2(n + 1)}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\log_2(2)} - \dfrac{1}{\log_2(256)} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{7}{8} \end{aligned}$
by telescoping. Therefore, the answer is $\boxed{{\textbf{(C)}~\dfrac{7}{8}}}$.

raw_content.title: There are integers $a$ and $b$ such that the polynomial $x^{3}-5x^{2}+ax+b$ has $4+\sqrt{5}$ as a root. What is $a+b?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Since $4 + \sqrt{5}$ is a root and all the coefficients are integers, the conjugate $4 - \sqrt{5}$ must also be a root. By Vieta's, the roots sum to $5$, so the last root must be $-3$. Hence the polynomial must be:

$(x^2 - 8x + 11)(x + 3) = x^3 - 5x^2 - 13x + 33$
and so $(a, b) = (-13, 33)$. This yields a final answer of $\boxed{{\textbf{(C)~20}}}$.

Alternate Solution:

Suppose $P(x)$ was the desired polynomial. Then $P(1) = a + b - 4$. We found the roots to be $4 + \sqrt{5}$, $4 - \sqrt{5}$, and $-3$, so we could calculate:

$a + b - 4 = \left(1 - \left(4 + \sqrt{5}\right)\right)\left(1 - \left(4 - \sqrt{5}\right)\right)\left(1 - \left(-3\right)\right) = (-\sqrt{5} - 3)(\sqrt{5} - 3)(4) = 16$
and so $a + b = 20$, which leads to the same as before.

raw_content.title: What is the tens digit of $6^{6^{6}}?$

solution_info.solution_info:
The last two digits of powers of $6$ cycle as follows:

$06 \to 36 \to 16 \to 96 \to 76 \to 56 \to 36 \to 16 \to \dots$
This cycle has period $5$. Since $6^6 \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$, we have that $6^{6^6} \equiv 56 \pmod{100}$, so the tens digit is $\boxed{{\textbf{(C)~5}}}$.

Alternate Solution:

We wish to calculate $6^{6^6} \pmod{100}$. Note that $6^{6^6} \equiv 0 \pmod{4}$. Since $6^5 \equiv 1 \pmod{25}$, we must have $6^{6^6} \equiv 6 \pmod{25}$. By Chinese Remainder Theorem, it follows that $6^{6^6} \equiv 56 \pmod{100}$, and so the tens digit is $5$, as before.

raw_content.title: The altitude to the hypotenuse of a $30^\circ\!-\!60^\circ\!-\!90^\circ$ right triangle is divided into two segments of lengths $x<y$ by the median to the shortest side of the triangle. What is the ratio $\dfrac{x}{x+y}?$

solution_info.solution_info:
We will use mass points.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/108051583f5a296d5c19709a9f17b0efc14e58c5b08e0a611517bd9ce690c811.png]

Note that since $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle BEC$, we have

$CE=\dfrac{BC^2}{CA}=\dfrac{3}{4}$
as $\triangle ABC$ is a $30^\circ-60^\circ-90^\circ$ triangle.

Assign a mass of $3$ at $A$, which means we will assign a mass of $1$ at $C$. As $AD=DB$, this means $B$ has a mass of $3$ as well, so $E$ has a mass of $4$ and $F$ has a mass of $7$.

Thus

$\dfrac{FB}{EF}=\dfrac{\text{mass at } E}{\text{mass at } B}=\dfrac{4}{3}$
Thus $x=3,y=4$, and $\dfrac{x}{x+y}=\boxed{{\textbf{(A)}~\dfrac{3}{7}}}$.

While there is a simple solution with mass points, we defer to using areas.

Note that

$\dfrac{[CFB]}{[CEF]}=\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot FB\cdot\text{distance} \text{ from } C \text{ to } FB}{\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot EB\cdot\text{distance} \text{ from } C \text{ to } EF}=\dfrac{FB}{EF}$
as $FB$ and $EF$ are the same line. Note that

$\dfrac{[CEF]}{[CAF]}=\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot FE\cdot CE}{\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot FE\cdot CA}=\dfrac{CE}{CA}$
as $FE$ is perpendicular to $AC$. Note that

$[CAD]=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot AD\cdot CB=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot BD\cdot CB=[CBD]$
$[FAD]=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot AD\cdot\text{distance} \text{ from } F \text{ to } AD=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot BD\cdot \text{distance} \text{ from } F \text{ to } BD=[FBD]$
so $[AFC]=[ACD]-[AFD]=[BCD]-[BFC]=[CFB]$. Thus, combining these we get

$\dfrac{FB}{EF}=\dfrac{[CFB]}{[CEF]}=\dfrac{[AFC]}{[CEF]}=\dfrac{CA}{CE}$
Note that since $\triangle ABC\sim\triangle BEC$, we have

$CE=\dfrac{BC^2}{CA}=\dfrac{3}{4}$
as $\triangle ABC$ is a $30-60-90$ triangle, hence

$\dfrac{FB}{EF}=\dfrac{4}{3}$
Thus $x=3,y=4$, and $\dfrac{x}{x+y}=\boxed{{\textbf{(A)}~\dfrac{3}{7}}}$.

raw_content.title: Nine athletes, no two of whom are the same height, try out for the basketball team. One at a time, they draw a wristband at random, without replacement, from a bag containing $3$ blue bands, $3$ red bands, and $3$ green bands. They are divided into a blue group, a red group, and a green group. The tallest member of each group is named the group captain. What is the probability that the group captains are the three tallest athletes?

solution_info.solution_info:
Without loss of generality, suppose the $3$ tallest athletes draw first. The condition is equivalent to saying they must all draw different colored wristbands. Regardless of which color band the first person draws, the second person has a $\dfrac{6}{8}$ chance to draw a different colored band on their draw. The third person then has a $\dfrac{3}{7}$ chance to draw a band different from the other two. Thus the final answer is

$\dfrac{6}{8}\cdot \dfrac{3}{7}=\boxed{{\textbf{(C)}~~\dfrac{9}{28}}}$

raw_content.title:
Consider a decreasing sequence of $n$ positive integers $x_{1}>x_{2}>\cdots>x_{n}$ that satisfies:

The average of the first $3$ terms is $2025$.

For all $4\le k\le n$, the average of the first $k$ terms is $1$ less than the average of the first $k-1$ terms.

What is the greatest possible value of $n?$

solution_info.solution_info:
From the second condition, we have that the average of the first $4$ terms is $2024$, the average of the first $5$ terms is $2023$... so inductively the average of the first $k$ terms is $2028-k$. This also implies that the sum of the first $k$ terms is $k(2028-k)$.

If we know the partial sums of a sequence, we may recover the terms by subtracting two adjacent terms. In other words, the $k$th term of this sequence is the sum of the first $k$ terms minus the sum of the first $k-1$ terms. This gives us:

$x_k = k(2028-k) - (k-1)(2028 - (k-1))$
$= (2028k - k^2) - (-2029 + 2030k - k^2) = 2029 - 2k$
As the terms must be positive: $x_k > 0 \implies 2029 > 2k \implies k < 1014.5$ gives us the maximum possible value of $n$ as

$\boxed{{\textbf{(B)~1014}}}$.

Additionally, note that since $a_4 = 2021$, it is possible to assign values to $a_1$, $a_2$, and $a_3$ which does not affect the bound later down the line.

raw_content.title: An analog clock starts at midnight and runs for $2025$ minutes before stopping. What is the tangent of the acute angle between the hour hand and the minute hand when the clock stops?

solution_info.solution_info:
$2025$ minutes corresponds to $33$ hours and $45$ minutes, so the analog clock will show $9:45$.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/339529b76c8c3d6a9eef59a88f163978959484303d55e75a13bb590c4ea23484.png]

Hence, the angle between the hour and minute hand is $\dfrac{3}{4} \cdot 30^{\circ} = 22.5^{\circ}$. We can use the half-angle formula to calculate:

$\tan 22.5^{\circ} = \dfrac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{1 + \cos 45^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}/2}{1 + \sqrt{2}/{2}} = \sqrt{2} - 1$
so the answer is $\boxed{{\textbf{(B)}~\sqrt{2} - 1}}$.

raw_content.title: Awnik repeatedly plays a game that has a probability of winning of $\dfrac{1}{3}$. The outcomes are independent. What is the expected value of the number of games he will play until he has both won and lost at least once?

solution_info.solution_info:
After the first game, there is a $\dfrac{1}{3}$ chance he has won a game and a $\dfrac{2}{3}$ chance he has lost a game. If he has won, then he plays until he loses a game, so in expectation, he will play $\dfrac{1}{2/3} = \dfrac{3}{2}$ more games. If he has lost, then he plays until he wins a game, so in expectation, he will play $\dfrac{1}{1/3} = 3$ more games. Hence, the expected value of the number of additional games he will play is given by:

$\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[\text{additional games}] &= \mathbb P\left(\text{win 1st game}\right) \cdot \mathbb E[\text{additional games} \mid \text{win 1st game}] \\ & \hspace{3.5mm} + \mathbb P\left(\text{lose 1st game}\right) \cdot \mathbb E[\text{additional games} \mid \text{lose 1st game}] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{2}{3} \cdot 3 = \dfrac{5}{2} \end{aligned}$
Hence, including the first game, Awnik will play $\dfrac{7}{2}$ games on average, which corresponds to $\boxed{{\textbf{(D)}~\dfrac{7}{2}}}$.

raw_content.title: A rectangular grid of squares has $141$ rows and $91$ columns. Each square has room for two numbers. Horace and Vera each fill in the grid with the numbers $1$ through $141\times 91=12{,}831$. Horace fills horizontally (left to right within each row); Vera fills vertically (top to bottom within each column). How many squares get two copies of the same number?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $(x,y)$ represent the column and row at which the two numbers are equal.

$H = 91(y-1) + x$
$V = 141(x-1) + y$
Equating, we get $91(y-1) + x = 141(x-1) + y$, or

$91y - 91 + x = 141x - 141 + y \implies 140x - 90y = 50 \implies 14x - 9y = 5.$
Working $\text{mod } 9$, we get

$14x - 9y \equiv 5 \pmod{9} \implies 5x \equiv 5 \pmod{9} \implies x \equiv 1 \pmod{9}.$
Let $x = 9k + 1$. Then,

$14(9k + 1) - 9y = 5 \implies 9y = 14 \cdot 9k + 14 - 5 = 126k + 9 \implies y = 14k + 1.$
We require

$1 \le x \le 91 \implies 1 \le 9k + 1 \le 91 \implies 0 \le k \le 10$
$1 \le y \le 141 \implies 1 \le 14k + 1 \le 141 \implies 0 \le k \le 10.$
Thus there are a total of $11$ values of $k$, implying there are $\boxed{{\textbf{(C)~11}}}$ cells where both of them write the same number.

raw_content.title:
A frog hops along the number line according to the following rules:

It starts at $0$.

If it is at $0$, then it moves to $1$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and disappears with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

For $n=1,2,3$, if it is at $n$, then it moves to $n+1$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, to $n-1$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, and disappears with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

What is the probability that the frog reaches $4?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Let $p_n$ be the probability that the frog eventually reaches $4$ given that it starts at position $n$.

Once the frog reaches $4$, we are done, so

$p_4 = 1.$
From $0$, the frog either moves to $1$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$ or disappears with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$p_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} p_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0 = \dfrac{1}{2} p_1.$
For $n = 1,2,3$, from position $n$ the frog moves to $n+1$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, to $n-1$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, and disappears with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$, so

$p_n = \dfrac{1}{4} p_{n+1} + \dfrac{1}{4} p_{n-1} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 0 = \dfrac{1}{4}(p_{n+1} + p_{n-1}).$
Writing these explicitly for $n=1,2,3$ and using $p_4 = 1$ gives

$\left\{ \begin{aligned} p_0 &= \dfrac{1}{2} p_1,\\ p_1 &= \dfrac{1}{4}(p_2 + p_0),\\ p_2 &= \dfrac{1}{4}(p_3 + p_1),\\ p_3 &= \dfrac{1}{4}(p_4 + p_2) = \dfrac{1}{4}(1 + p_2). \end{aligned}\right.$
From $p_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} p_1$ we have

$p_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} p_1.$
Substitute into the equation for $p_1$:

$p_1 = \dfrac{1}{4}\bigl(p_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} p_1\bigr) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4p_1 = p_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} p_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 8p_1 = 2p_2 + p_1.$
Thus

$7p_1 = 2p_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_2 = \dfrac{7}{2}p_1.$
Use $p_2$ in the equation for $p_2$:

$p_2 = \dfrac{1}{4}(p_3 + p_1) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4p_2 = p_3 + p_1.$
Substitute $p_2 = \dfrac{7}{2} p_1$:

$4\cdot \dfrac{7}{2} p_1 = p_3 + p_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 14p_1 = p_3 + p_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_3 = 13p_1.$
Now use the equation for $p_3$:

$p_3 = \dfrac{1}{4}(1 + p_2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4p_3 = 1 + p_2.$
Substitute $p_3 = 13p_1$ and $p_2 = \dfrac{7}{2} p_1$:

$4\cdot 13p_1 = 1 + \dfrac{7}{2} p_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 52p_1 = 1 + \dfrac{7}{2} p_1.$
We can further simplify with

$\dfrac{104}{2}p_1 = 1 + \dfrac{7}{2} p_1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left(\dfrac{104}{2} - \dfrac{7}{2}\right) p_1 = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{97}{2}p_1 = 1.$
Hence

$p_1 = \dfrac{2}{97}.$
Finally, from $p_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} p_1$,

$p_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \dfrac{2}{97} = \dfrac{1}{97}.$
Therefore, the probability that the frog reaches $4$ is

$\boxed{{\textbf{(E)~$\dfrac{1}{97}$}}}$
Alternate Solution (using a transition table / Markov chain).

We model the frog as a Markov chain with the following states:

$0,1,2,3,4,D,$
where $D$ is a "dead" state (the frog disappeared). We treat $4$ and $D$ as absorbing states: once the frog reaches $4$ or disappears, it stays there forever for the purposes of this problem.

From the rules of the problem, the one-step transition probabilities are:

$\begin{array}{c|cccccc} \text{From} \backslash \text{To} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & D \\ \hline 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \\ \hline 1 & \frac{1}{4} & 0 & \frac{1}{4} & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \\ \hline 2 & 0 & \frac{1}{4} & 0 & \frac{1}{4} & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \\ \hline 3 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{4} & 0 & \frac{1}{4} & \frac{1}{2} \\ \hline 4 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \hline D & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}$
Let $p_n$ be the probability that the frog is eventually absorbed in state $4$ (i.e., eventually reaches $4$) given that it starts in state $n$.

For the absorbing states:

$p_4 = 1, \qquad p_D = 0.$
For a non-absorbing state $n$, the Markov property gives

$p_n = \sum_{\text{states } s} P(\text{go from }n\text{ to }s \text{ in one step}) \cdot p_s.$
Using the rows of the transition table:

From $0$: it goes to $1$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and to $D$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$p_0 = \dfrac{1}{2} p_1 + \dfrac{1}{2} p_D = \dfrac{1}{2} p_1.$

From $1$: it goes to $0$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, to $2$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, and to $D$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$p_1 = \dfrac{1}{4} p_0 + \dfrac{1}{4} p_2 + \dfrac{1}{2} p_D = \dfrac{1}{4}(p_0 + p_2).$

From $2$:

$p_2 = \dfrac{1}{4} p_1 + \dfrac{1}{4} p_3.$

From $3$: it goes to $2$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, to $4$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$, and to $D$ with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$p_3 = \dfrac{1}{4} p_2 + \dfrac{1}{4} p_4 + \dfrac{1}{2} p_D = \dfrac{1}{4} p_2 + \dfrac{1}{4}.$
Thus, we again obtain the system

$\left\{ \begin{aligned} p_0 &= \dfrac{1}{2} p_1,\\ p_1 &= \dfrac{1}{4}(p_0 + p_2),\\ p_2 &= \dfrac{1}{4}(p_1 + p_3),\\ p_3 &= \dfrac{1}{4}(p_2 + 1). \end{aligned}\right.$
We can regard this as a linear system coming from the transition table, and solve it systematically (for example, by substitution as in Solution 1, or by Gaussian elimination on the augmented matrix). Solving yields

$p_0 = \dfrac{1}{97}.$
Therefore, by the table/Markov-chain method as well, the probability that the frog reaches $4$ is

$\boxed{{\textbf{(E)~$\dfrac{1}{97}$}}}$

raw_content.title: Two non-congruent triangles have the same area. Each triangle has sides of length $8$ and $9$, and the third side of each triangle has integer length. What is the sum of the lengths of the third sides?

solution_info.solution_info:
Let the triangles have side lengths $8-9-m$ and $8-9-n$. By Heron's formula, we must have:

$\sqrt{\dfrac{m + 8 + 9}{2} \cdot \dfrac{m + 8 - 9}{2} \cdot \dfrac{m + 9 - 8}{2} \cdot \dfrac{8 + 9 - m}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{n + 8 + 9}{2} \cdot \dfrac{n + 8 - 9}{2} \cdot \dfrac{n + 9 - 8}{2} \cdot \dfrac{8 + 9 - n}{2}}$
Hence, the following polynomial has least two distinct positive integer roots (namely $m$ and $n$):

$P(x) = - (17 + x)(17 - x)(x + 1)(x - 1) + c$
where $c$ is some real number. Note that $P(x) = (x^2 - 1)(x^2 - 289) + c = x^4 - 290x^2 + (289 + c)$ is even, so its four roots are $m$, $-m$, $n$, and $-n$. Hence $m^2 + n^2 = 290$ for some $m$ and $n$ satisfying $1 < m, n < 17$. We can solve this by inspection and see that $m$ and $n$ must be $11$ and $13$ in some order, which yields a final answer of $\boxed{{\textbf{(C)~24}}}$.

Remark: We can verify that the area of a $8-9-11$ triangle is the same as the area of a $8-9-13$ triangle, namely $6\sqrt{35}$.

raw_content.title: What is the greatest possible area of the triangle in the complex plane with vertices $2z$, $(1+i)z$, and $(1-i)z$, where $z$ satisfies $|4z-2|=1?$

solution_info.solution_info:
[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/336517a57f17c9e93f1c2f25ded41fa0c0aebd9434646bb8fa8e3c8e823f384a.png]

Note that $\left|4z-2\right| = 1$ represents a circle with center $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (denoted by point $X$ in the diagram above) and radius $\dfrac{1}{4}$. Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be the vertices of the triangle, and let $O$ be the origin. Then $OBAC$ always forms a square, whose side length is always $\left|(1 + i)z\right| = \sqrt{2} \cdot \left|z\right|$. Hence, the area of the triangle is always equal to $\left|z\right|^2$.

To maximize this area, it is sufficient to maximize $\left|z\right|$ i.e. maximize $OZ$. Since $OZ \leq OX + XZ = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{4}$, the maximum possible area is $\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{16}$, which corresponds to $\boxed{{\textbf{(C)}~\dfrac{9}{16}}}$.

Alternate Solution:

Consider the triangle with vertices $2$, $1 + i$, and $1 - i$, with area $1$. Then the triangle with vertices $2z$, $(1 + i)z$, and $(1 - i)z$ is a transformation of the original triangle, where we dilate it by a factor of $\left|z\right|$ and rotate it counterclockwise by an angle of $\text{arg}(z)$. Hence, by similar triangles, its new area is $\left|z\right|^2$. The rest of the solution follows as above.

raw_content.title: Let $S$ be the set of all integers $z>1$ such that for all pairs of nonnegative integers $(x,y)$ with $x<y<z$, the remainder when $2025x$ is divided by $z$ is less than the remainder when $2025y$ is divided by $z$. What is the sum of the elements of $S?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Define $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ to be the "fractional part" of a number and let $\alpha = \left\{\dfrac{2025}{z}\right\}$. Note that the given condition is equivalent to:

$\left\{\dfrac{2025}{z}\right\}, \left\{2 \cdot \dfrac{2025}{z}\right\}, \dots, \left\{(z - 1) \cdot \dfrac{2025}{z}\right\}$
being a strictly increasing sequence.

If $\alpha = 0$, then the sequence is identically zero, which fails. If $\alpha > \dfrac{1}{z}$, then there exist $k$ and $k + 1$ such that:

$\left\{\dfrac{2025k}{z}\right\} = k\alpha \qquad \left\{\dfrac{2025(k + 1)}{z}\right\} = (k + 1)\alpha - 1$
Since $\alpha < 1$, we must have $k\alpha > (k + 1)\alpha - 1$, and so this violates the condition for the pair $(k, k + 1)$.

Hence, we must have $0 < \alpha \leq \dfrac{1}{z}$, which implies that the condition is equivalent to the fact remainder when $2025$ is divided by $z$ is equal to $1$. Therefore, $z$ can be any factor of $2024$ that is greater than $1$. Note that the sum of the factors of $2024 = 2^3 \cdot 11 \cdot 23$ is given by $15 \cdot 12 \cdot 24 = 4320$, and so the desired answer is $4320 - 1 = 4319$, which corresponds to $\boxed{{\textbf{(E)~4319}}}$.

raw_content.title: How many real numbers satisfy the equation $\sin(20\pi x)=\log_{20}x?$

solution_info.solution_info:
We must have that $-1 \leq \log_{20}(x) \leq 1$, so $\dfrac{1}{20} \leq x \leq 20$. The period of $\sin(20\pi x)$ is $\dfrac{2\pi}{20\pi} = \dfrac{1}{10}$, so in the range $[0, 20]$, the sine curve has $200$ full periods of the form $\left[\dfrac{k}{10}, \dfrac{k + 1}{10}\right]$ for $0 \leq k < 200$.

Note that in each period, there are two distinct intersections. This includes the final period, since at $x = 20$, the log curve is at $1$, while the sine curve is at $0$ i.e. the situation as follows:

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/3ba3edcae27b57d73e3ab2bedb74a69b7fb6687e66ada232e57038a64d80802e.png]

However, one of the intersections (namely $(1, 0)$) is a part of two different periods, and so it is double-counted, as shown below.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/d2f57d7b0ed43beb2822188c0788753f45daec532401de1072205724bda773e7.png]

Hence, the total number of intersection points if $2 \cdot 200 - 1 = 399$, which corresponds to $\boxed{{\textbf{(D)~399}}}$.

raw_content.title: Three concentric circles have radii $1,2,3$. An equilateral triangle with side length $s$ has one vertex on each circle. What is $s^{2}?$

solution_info.solution_info:
Suppose $A$, $B$, and $C$ are the vertices of the equilateral triangle on the circles of radius $1$, $2$, and $3$, and suppose that point $X$ is the center of the concentric circles, so that our diagram is as follows:

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/7be60b8955e89f17710b93de5df68207b7a2bca8c2f8c1a58e50c06780f5fc8d.png]

Since $CX \cdot AB = AX \cdot BC + BX \cdot AC$, we must have that $X$ lies on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, by the converse of Ptolemy's theorem. This is depicted below.

[Figure: /question-assets/source/amc/6ed1c7cfb2e3440a944a4c6ece21ca02ae799a1903ef4642d896798ce0b639ee.png]

Hence, $\angle AXB = 120^{\circ}$. Since $AX = 1$ and $BX = 2$, we have that:

$s^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 - 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 7$
by Law of Cosines, so the answer is $\boxed{{\textbf{(E)~7}}}$.
